title: Contains Duplicate
desc: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice, and false if every element is distinct.
hints: Comparing every pair works, but it takes O(n²) time. Can you remember what you have already seen?
A hash set answers 'have I seen this value?' in O(1).
Alternative: sort the array first, then only neighbours can be equal.
editorial: Walk through the array and keep a set of values seen so far. If the current value is already in the set, a duplicate exists. Otherwise add it and move on.
Sorting also works (check adjacent pairs) at O(n log n) time with no extra set, which is a useful trade-off when memory is tight.

title: Valid Anagram
desc: Given two lowercase strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, meaning it uses exactly the same letters the same number of times in any order.
constraints: s and t contain only lowercase English letters
hints: If the lengths differ, the answer is immediately false.
Two strings are anagrams when every letter has the same count in both.
Only 26 letters exist, so a fixed-size count array is enough.
editorial: Count how many times each letter occurs in s, then walk through t and subtract. If a count would go below zero, t has a letter that s does not have enough of.
Sorting both strings and comparing also works, at O(n log n).

title: Two Sum
desc:
Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target.

Exactly one valid pair exists, and you may not use the same element twice. The indices can be returned in any order.
hints: Checking all pairs is O(n²). What if, for each number, you looked up the number you still need?
For x, the partner is target - x.
Store each value's index in a hash map as you scan, and check the map before inserting.
editorial: Scan left to right with a map from value to index. For the current value x, if target - x is already in the map, you found the pair. Otherwise store x and continue.
Checking before inserting guarantees you never pair an element with itself, and the whole thing is a single pass.

title: Valid Parentheses
desc:
Given a string s made only of the characters ( ) [ ] { }, return true if it is valid.

A string is valid when every opening bracket is closed by the same type of bracket, and brackets close in the correct order.
hints: The most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed.
That last-in, first-out behaviour is exactly what a stack gives you.
At the end the stack must be empty, otherwise some bracket was never closed.
editorial: Push every opening bracket on a stack. When you see a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener; pop it, or return false if it does not match or the stack is empty.
After the scan the stack must be empty. Leftover openers mean unclosed brackets.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
desc:
prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You may buy on one day and sell on a later day, once.

Return the maximum profit you can make. If no profit is possible, return 0.
hints: Trying every buy/sell pair is O(n²).
For a fixed selling day, the best buying day is the cheapest day before it.
Keep the lowest price seen so far while scanning.
editorial: Scan once, tracking the minimum price so far. At each day, the best profit selling today is price - minSoFar. Keep the maximum of those.
This is a tiny sliding-window idea: the left edge is the cheapest day, the right edge is today.
solution:
def maxProfit(prices):
    best = 0
    low = prices[0]
    for p in prices:
        low = min(low, p)
        best = max(best, p - low)
    return best

title: Binary Search
desc:
Given an array nums sorted in ascending order with distinct values, and an integer target, return the index of target, or -1 if it is not present.

Your solution must run in O(log n) time.
constraints: All values are distinct and sorted ascending
hints: A linear scan is O(n). The array being sorted lets you do much better.
Look at the middle element. Is the target in the left half or the right half?
Keep two boundaries lo and hi and shrink them until they cross.
editorial: Compare the middle element with the target. If equal, return it. If the middle is smaller, the target can only be on the right, so move lo past mid; otherwise move hi before mid.
Each step halves the search range, so at most about log2(n) steps are needed. Use lo + (hi - lo) / 2 in C++/Java to avoid overflow.

title: Climbing Stairs
desc:
You are climbing a staircase with n steps. Each move you can climb either 1 or 2 steps.

Return the number of distinct ways to reach the top.
hints: Think about the very last move. From which steps could you have arrived at step n?
ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2).
Plain recursion repeats work exponentially. Remember results, or just keep the last two.
editorial: To land on step n, your last move was from step n-1 (a 1-step) or from n-2 (a 2-step). So ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), which is the Fibonacci sequence.
Compute it bottom-up, keeping only the previous two values. A naive recursive version without memoization takes exponential time and will time out for n = 45.

title: Majority Element
desc:
Given an integer array nums of length n, return the value that appears more than n / 2 times.

The input is guaranteed to contain such a value, so there is always exactly one answer. A solution that uses O(1) extra space is possible.
constraints: A value occurring more than nums.length / 2 times always exists
hints: Counting every value with a hash map works. Can you do it without the map?
The majority value outnumbers all the other values put together.
Keep one candidate and a counter: same value as the candidate adds one, a different value subtracts one, and a counter of zero lets the next element become the candidate.
editorial: Use the Boyer-Moore voting idea. Hold a candidate and a counter. For each element, if the counter is zero take the element as the new candidate; then add one if it equals the candidate and subtract one otherwise. Every subtraction cancels one majority element against one non-majority element, and since the majority has more than half of all elements, it is the one left standing.

A hash map of counts is simpler and also O(n) time, at the cost of O(n) space. Sorting the array and reading the middle element works too, because the majority value must cover the middle position, but it costs O(n log n).

title: Single Number
desc:
In the integer array nums, every value appears exactly twice except for one value that appears exactly once. Return that single value.

Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
constraints: Exactly one value appears once; all others appear exactly twice
hints: A hash set or a count map solves it, but uses O(n) memory.
What happens when you combine a number with itself using XOR (^)? And with 0?
XOR is commutative and associative, so XOR-ing the whole array cancels every pair and leaves the single value.
editorial: For any x, x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. XOR also does not care about order. So XOR-ing all elements together makes each pair vanish and leaves exactly the value that has no partner.

The set approach (add on first sight, remove on second) or a sum trick such as 2 * sum(set(nums)) - sum(nums) also works, but both need O(n) extra memory and the sum version can overflow in fixed-width integer types. XOR never overflows.

title: Missing Number
desc:
The array nums holds n distinct integers, each taken from the range 0..n inclusive. That range has n + 1 numbers, so exactly one of them is absent. Return the absent number.

The array may be in any order. Try to use O(1) extra space.
hints: Putting everything in a set and testing 0..n works. Is there a way to avoid the set?
You know which numbers should be there: all of 0..n. Compare that with what is there.
Either subtract sum(nums) from n(n+1)/2, or XOR all indices 0..n together with all values.
editorial: The sum of 0..n is n(n+1)/2. Subtract the sum of the array and the difference is the missing number. In fixed-width languages, the sum stays tiny for n ≤ 10,000, so there is no overflow concern here.

A more overflow-proof variant XORs every index from 0 to n with every array value; each present number appears twice and cancels, leaving the missing one. Sorting and looking for the first index where nums[i] != i also works at O(n log n).

title: Valid Palindrome
desc:
The string s contains letters (upper or lower case), digits and the dash character -. Ignore every dash and ignore the difference between upper and lower case. Return true if what remains reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise return false.

A string with nothing left after ignoring dashes counts as a palindrome.
constraints: s contains only letters, digits and '-'
hints: You could build a cleaned copy and compare it with its reverse. Can you compare in place instead?
Put one pointer at each end and compare the characters they point to.
Before each comparison, move a pointer inward while it sits on a dash. Compare the lower-cased characters.
editorial: Start with i = 0 and j = n - 1. Move i forward while s[i] is a dash, and j backward while s[j] is a dash. If the pointers have not crossed, the lower-cased characters must match; if they do not, return false. Otherwise step both inward and repeat until the pointers meet.

Building the cleaned, lower-cased string and comparing it with its reverse is just as correct and easier to write, but it allocates O(n) extra memory. The two-pointer version uses O(1) extra space and stops at the first mismatch.

title: Is Subsequence
desc:
Return true if string s is a subsequence of string t, and false otherwise.

A subsequence is obtained by deleting zero or more characters from t without changing the order of the characters that remain. The empty string is a subsequence of every string.
constraints: s and t contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Try to match the characters of s inside t one after the other, in order.
Use a pointer i into s. Scan t from left to right.
Whenever t[j] == s[i], advance i. At the end, s is a subsequence exactly when i reached the length of s.
editorial: Walk through t once. Keep an index i of the next character of s still to be matched. If the current character of t equals s[i], matching greedily is always safe, so increment i. If i reaches len(s) every character was matched in order.

Matching each character at its earliest possible position never hurts later characters, which is why the greedy scan is correct. The cost is a single pass over t. (If you had to answer many queries against the same t, you would precompute for each position the next occurrence of each letter instead.)

title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
desc:
A staircase has steps numbered 0 to n - 1, and cost[i] is the toll you pay every time you step on step i. You may start on step 0 or on step 1 (paying that step's toll), and from any step you can climb either 1 or 2 steps.

The top of the staircase is the position just past the last step, n. Return the minimum total toll you must pay to reach the top.
hints: Consider the last step you stand on before reaching the top. Which steps could that be?
Let best(i) be the cheapest total toll for a trip that ends by standing on step i (including cost[i]). Then best(i) = cost[i] + min(best(i-1), best(i-2)).
The answer is the cheaper of best(n-1) and best(n-2). You only need the previous two values, so two variables are enough.
editorial: Define best(i) as the minimum toll to stand on step i, tolls included. You can start on step 0 or 1, so best(0) = cost[0] and best(1) = cost[1]. For later steps you arrived from i-1 or i-2, so best(i) = cost[i] + min(best(i-1), best(i-2)). The top can be reached from step n-1 or n-2, so the answer is min(best(n-1), best(n-2)).
Computing it bottom-up while keeping only the last two values uses O(1) extra space. A recursion without memoisation re-solves the same steps over and over and takes exponential time.

title: Pascal's Triangle
desc: Build the first numRows rows of Pascal's triangle and return them as a list of rows. Row i (counting from 0) has i + 1 entries. The first and last entry of every row are 1, and every other entry is the sum of the two entries directly above it in the previous row.
hints: Write out the first five rows on paper and look at how each number relates to the row above.
Row 0 is [1]. For row i, entry j is the sum of entries j-1 and j of row i-1 (treat missing neighbours as 0).
Start every row with 1, add the pairwise sums of the previous row, and end with 1.
editorial: Build the triangle row by row. The new row begins with 1, then for each adjacent pair (prev[j-1], prev[j]) in the previous row it appends their sum, and it ends with 1. This is a direct dynamic program where each row depends only on the row before it.

Another way is the closed form C(i, j) = C(i, j-1) * (i - j + 1) / j, which creates each row without looking at the previous one. For 30 rows every value fits comfortably in a 32-bit integer (the largest is 77,558,760).

title: Plus One
desc:
A non-negative integer is stored as an array digits with the most significant digit first, one digit per element. The number has no leading zeros, except for the number zero itself, which is stored as [0].

Add one to the number and return its digits in the same format. You may not convert the whole array to a single integer, because the number can have thousands of digits.
constraints: digits[0] is not 0 unless the array is exactly [0]
hints: Add one the way you would on paper: start from the last digit.
If the last digit is below 9, just increase it and you are done. If it is 9, it becomes 0 and a carry moves left.
If the carry falls off the front (all digits were 9), the result needs one extra leading 1.
editorial: Scan from the right. Each digit that equals 9 turns into 0 and passes the carry on; the first digit that is not 9 is increased by one and the answer is ready. Usually this stops after a single step.
Only when every digit is 9 does the loop run to the end. The answer is then a 1 followed by all zeros, so we build it directly. The array is processed once, which is optimal.

title: Integer Square Root
desc:
Given a non-negative integer x, return the square root of x rounded down to the nearest integer, that is the largest integer r with r × r ≤ x.

Do not use floating-point numbers, pow, sqrt or any similar built-in.
hints: Trying r = 0, 1, 2, ... until r² exceeds x works, but how many steps is that for large x?
The condition 'r × r ≤ x' is true for small r and false for large r. That is a sorted yes/no pattern you can binary search.
Search r between 0 and x. Compare mid with x / mid instead of multiplying, so that mid × mid cannot overflow a 32-bit integer.
editorial: The predicate r*r ≤ x is monotone: true up to the answer, false afterwards. Binary search for the last r where it holds. For x ≥ 1 the answer is at most x, and a safe test that avoids overflow is mid ≤ x / mid using integer division.

Newton's iteration r = (r + x / r) / 2 converges even faster, in a handful of steps, but needs care with the stopping rule. The linear scan is only fine for tiny x because the answer can be as large as 46,340.

title: First Unique Character
desc:
Given a string s, find the first character that occurs exactly once in the whole string and return its index (0-based). If every character repeats, return -1.

For example, in "planet" every letter is unique, so the answer is 0; in "aabcb" the answer is 3; in "abab" the answer is -1.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Checking each character against all the others works, but is slow for long strings. What do you need to know about each character?
You only need to know how many times each letter occurs in the entire string.
Make one pass to count the letters, then a second pass from the left to return the first index whose letter has count 1.
editorial: Count the occurrences of every character with a hash map (or an array of 26 counters) in one pass. Then scan the string from the left a second time and return the first index whose character has a count of exactly one. If the scan ends without a hit, return -1.

Comparing every character with every other character is O(n²) and becomes slow at 50,000 characters. The two-pass counting approach is linear, and the counter table has constant size because the alphabet is fixed.

title: Isomorphic Strings
desc:
Two strings s and t of the same length are isomorphic if you can rename the characters of s to get exactly t. A renaming assigns each distinct character of s one replacement character, and two different characters of s are never given the same replacement. The order of the characters is preserved.

For example "egg" and "add" are isomorphic (e→a, g→d), but "foo" and "bar" are not (the two os would need different replacements), and neither are "ab" and "cc" (two characters would share one replacement).

Return true if the strings are isomorphic.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase letters and digits
hints: Walking both strings together, each character of s must always meet the same character of t.
That one direction is not enough: "ab" vs "cc" passes it. The rule must also hold when you look from t back to s.
Keep two maps, s→t and t→s, and return false as soon as either one is contradicted.
editorial: Scan both strings at the same index. Store, for the pair (a, b), that a maps to b and that b maps back to a. If a was already mapped to something other than b, or b was already the image of something other than a, the strings are not isomorphic.

An equivalent trick is to normalise each string by replacing every character with the index of its first occurrence, and compare the two normalised sequences. Both approaches run in linear time; the mapping tables have at most 36 entries because of the alphabet.

title: Run-Length Compressed Length
desc:
A run is a maximal block of equal consecutive characters. To compress a string, replace every run by its character followed by the length of the run written in decimal, except that a run of length 1 is written as just the character (no number).

For example "aaabccdddd" is compressed to "a3bc2d4", and a run of twelve x characters becomes "x12". Return the length of the compressed string.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: You do not have to build the compressed string; its length is enough.
Split the string into runs. A run of length 1 contributes 1; a longer run contributes 1 plus the number of decimal digits of its length.
Scan with two indices: start a run at i, advance j while s[j] == s[i], add the contribution, then continue from j.
editorial: Walk through the string and find each run with a pair of indices. A run of length k costs one character for the letter, plus len(str(k)) more characters when k > 1. Summing over all runs gives the answer in a single linear pass.

Note that counts with several digits matter: a run of 10 to 99 letters adds two digits, 100 to 999 adds three, and so on. Forgetting this is the most common mistake. Building the output string explicitly also works, but wastes memory.
solution:
def compressedLength(s):
    total = 0
    n = len(s)
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        j = i
        while j < n and s[j] == s[i]:
            j += 1
        run = j - i
        total += 1
        if run > 1:
            total += len(str(run))
        i = j
    return total

title: Longest Palindrome by Rearranging
desc:
You are given a string s. Pick some of its characters (each character of s can be used at most once) and arrange them in any order to form a palindrome. Return the maximum possible length of such a palindrome.

For example, from "abccccdd" you can build "dccaccd" of length 7. From "abc" you can only build a single-character palindrome, so the answer is 1.
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters and digits
hints: In a palindrome, every character appears on both sides of the centre, except possibly one in the middle.
A character that occurs c times can contribute c characters if c is even, or c - 1 of them as pairs if c is odd.
If any character was left over (some count was odd), one of them can sit in the middle, adding 1.
editorial: Count every character. Each character contributes 2 * (count // 2) characters to the two halves of the palindrome. Add up those pair contributions. If the total is smaller than len(s), at least one character has an odd count and has one unused copy, so one of those can be placed in the centre and the answer is the total plus one.
Equivalently, the answer is len(s) minus the number of characters with an odd count, plus one if that number is positive. No actual arrangement needs to be built.

title: Search Insert Position
desc:
You are given a strictly increasing array nums and an integer target. Return the index at which target is found. If it is not present, return the index where it would have to be inserted so that the array stays sorted.

Your solution must run in O(log n) time.
constraints: nums is sorted in strictly increasing order (no duplicates)
hints: A linear scan finds the first element that is not smaller than the target, but it is too slow for the intended bound.
The answer is the number of elements strictly smaller than target. Because the array is sorted, those elements form a prefix.
Binary search for the first index whose value is ≥ target. Keep the search range half-open, [lo, hi), and return lo when it closes.
editorial: The insertion point is the first index i with nums[i] ≥ target, or n when no such index exists. This is a classic lower bound search. The predicate nums[i] ≥ target is false for a prefix and true for the rest, so we can binary search for the boundary.

Keep lo = 0, hi = n. While lo < hi, take mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if nums[mid] < target move lo = mid + 1, otherwise hi = mid. When the loop ends lo is the boundary. Each step halves the range, giving O(log n) time and O(1) space.

title: Move Zeroes
desc:
Given an integer array nums, move every 0 to the end while keeping the relative order of the non-zero values unchanged. Return the resulting array.

Try to do the rearrangement in a single pass with O(1) extra space, by working in place on the array you were given.
hints: Collecting the non-zero values into a new list and padding with zeros works, but uses extra memory.
Use a write pointer that marks where the next non-zero value belongs. Everything before it is already final.
Scan with a read pointer. Whenever nums[read] is non-zero, swap it with nums[write] and advance write.
editorial: Keep two pointers. write is the position where the next non-zero element must be placed; read scans the array. When nums[read] != 0, swap it into nums[write] and advance write. All indices below write hold the non-zero values seen so far, in their original order, and everything between write and read is a zero.
Swapping (rather than copying and then filling with zeros) means each element is touched a constant number of times and zeros drift to the right automatically. Time is O(n), space O(1).

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
desc:
The array nums is sorted in non-decreasing order. Remove the duplicates so that every distinct value appears exactly once, keeping the values in order. Return the resulting array.

Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra space by overwriting the array in place.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Equal values are adjacent because the array is sorted, so a duplicate is just an element equal to its predecessor.
Keep a slow pointer at the end of the deduplicated prefix and a fast pointer that scans ahead.
When nums[fast] differs from nums[slow], advance slow and copy the value there. The answer is the first slow + 1 elements.
editorial: Since equal values are grouped together, each new distinct value is the first element after a run of equal ones. Let slow point at the last value kept. For each fast from 1 onward, if nums[fast] != nums[slow] then it is a new value: increment slow and write nums[fast] into that slot.

At the end the first slow + 1 positions hold the distinct values in order. The array is scanned once, so time is O(n); only two indices are used, so space is O(1) beyond the returned slice. Remember to handle the empty array.

title: Number of 1 Bits
desc:
Given a 32-bit signed integer n, return how many bits are set to 1 in its 32-bit two's complement representation.

For example, 11 is 00000000000000000000000000001011, which has three set bits, and -1 has all 32 bits set.
constraints: Negative numbers use the 32-bit two's complement representation
hints: Look at the lowest bit with n & 1, then shift right and repeat. How many times do you need to repeat?

Negative numbers are a trap in some languages: an arithmetic right shift keeps the sign bit, so the loop may never reach zero. Limit the loop to 32 steps, or first convert to an unsigned 32-bit value.
The expression n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit. Count how many times you can apply it before reaching zero.
editorial: The simplest method inspects each of the 32 bit positions: test (n >> i) & 1 for i from 0 to 31 and add up the results. Because the loop runs exactly 32 times, negative inputs need no special care.

A faster trick is Brian Kernighan's: n & (n - 1) removes exactly the lowest set bit, so repeating it until the value becomes zero takes as many steps as there are set bits. First mask the value to 32 bits (n & 0xFFFFFFFF) so negative numbers behave like their unsigned counterparts.
solution:
def hammingWeight(n):
    n &= 0xFFFFFFFF
    count = 0
    while n:
        n &= n - 1
        count += 1
    return count

title: Happy Number
desc:
Start with a positive integer n. Repeatedly replace it with the sum of the squares of its decimal digits. For instance, 19 becomes 1² + 9² = 82, then 8² + 2² = 68, and so on.

If this process eventually reaches 1, the number is happy. Otherwise it runs forever in a cycle that never contains 1. Return true if n is happy and false if not.
hints: Simulate the process. The difficulty is knowing when to stop for an unhappy number.
The sequence either reaches 1 or repeats a value it has visited before. A hash set of seen values detects the repeat.
After the first step the value is small (at most 810 for a 10-digit number), so a cycle must appear quickly. You can also detect it with slow and fast pointers and no extra memory.
editorial: Define next(x) as the sum of squared digits of x. A 10-digit number is mapped to at most 10 * 81 = 810, and every later value stays small, so the sequence lives in a tiny range. Hence it must either hit 1 (and then stay at 1) or enter a cycle.

Store each visited value in a set and stop when you reach 1 (answer true) or see a value again (answer false). To save memory, use Floyd's tortoise and hare: advance a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps; if they meet at a value other than 1 there is a cycle.

title: Last Stone Weight
desc:
You have a pile of stones, where stones[i] is the weight of the i-th stone. Play the following game until at most one stone remains:

  • Take the two heaviest stones, with weights x ≤ y.
  • If x == y, both stones are destroyed.
  • Otherwise the stone of weight x is destroyed and the other becomes a stone of weight y - x.

Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if no stones remain.
hints: Each round needs the two largest values. Re-sorting the whole array every round works but is slow.
A max-heap gives you the largest element in O(log n) and lets you insert new elements just as fast.
Pop two stones, push their difference back if it is non-zero, and stop when fewer than two stones remain.
editorial: Keep all weights in a max-heap. While at least two stones remain, pop the heaviest two, and if they differ push back their difference. Each round removes at least one stone, so there are fewer than n rounds, each costing O(log n).
Python's heapq is a min-heap, so store negated weights. Sorting the array every round is simpler but costs O(n² log n) overall.

title: Find the Town Judge
desc:
A town has n people labelled 1 to n. Rumour says one of them is the secret judge. If the judge exists, then:

  • the judge trusts nobody, and
  • everybody else trusts the judge.

You are given trust, where each entry [a, b] means that person a trusts person b. Anyone not listed as trusting someone trusts nobody.

Return the label of the judge, or -1 if there is no person who satisfies both rules.
constraints: trust[i] = [a, b] with 1 ≤ a, b ≤ n and a ≠ b
All pairs in trust are distinct
hints: The judge is the only person who can satisfy both rules, so at most one answer exists.
Think of each trust pair as a directed edge a → b. What do the in-degree and out-degree of the judge look like?
Keep one counter per person: subtract one when they trust someone and add one when someone trusts them. The judge ends with exactly n - 1.
editorial: Treat every pair as a directed edge from a to b. The judge has out-degree 0 and in-degree n - 1. Keep a single array score: decrement score[a] and increment score[b] for every pair.

A person who trusts anyone has a score of at most n - 2 (they cannot be trusted by everybody else and also trust someone). The judge scores exactly n - 1. So scan the array and return the person with score n - 1, or -1 if nobody has it. Because pairs are distinct, no one can be counted twice.

title: Unique Paths
desc:
A robot stands in the top-left cell of an m x n grid and wants to reach the bottom-right cell. In one move it can step either one cell down or one cell to the right; it can never leave the grid.

Return the number of different routes the robot can take. The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit signed integer.
hints: Look at the last move of any route. From which two cells can the robot arrive at the bottom-right cell?
Let ways[r][c] be the number of routes to cell (r, c). Then ways[r][c] = ways[r-1][c] + ways[r][c-1].
The first row and first column each have exactly one route. You only need the previous row to compute the next one, so one array of size n is enough.
editorial: Every route to cell (r, c) ends with a step from above or from the left, and those two groups of routes are disjoint. Hence ways[r][c] = ways[r-1][c] + ways[r][c-1], with the first row and first column equal to 1.

Because each row only depends on the row above, a single array updated left to right does the job: row[c] += row[c-1]. That is O(m · n) time and O(n) space. A route is also just a choice of which m - 1 of the m + n - 2 moves go down, giving the closed form C(m + n - 2, m - 1).

title: Set Mismatch
desc:
A list originally held every integer from 1 to n exactly once. Due to a data error, one of the numbers was overwritten by a copy of another number, so one value now appears twice and one value is missing entirely. The result is the array nums of length n.

Return a two-element array [duplicate, missing].

For example, [1, 2, 2, 4] gives [2, 3].
constraints: Exactly one value appears twice, exactly one value is missing, and every other value appears once
hints: Counting how many times each value in 1..n shows up tells you both answers directly.
You do not need a full map: a boolean marker per value (or a set of seen values) is enough to spot the repeat.
Once you know the duplicate d, the array sum equals n(n+1)/2 + d - missing, so the missing value follows from the sums.
editorial: Scan the array with a set. The first value that is already in the set is the duplicate. Because the array holds the numbers 1..n with the missing one replaced by the duplicate, sum(nums) = n(n+1)/2 - missing + duplicate, which gives missing = n(n+1)/2 - sum(nums) + duplicate.

A frequency array of size n+1 works just as well: the index with count 2 is the duplicate and the index with count 0 is the missing number. Both approaches are O(n) time. The sign-marking trick (negate nums[abs(x) - 1] on each visit) brings the extra space down to O(1).

title: Intersection of Two Arrays with Repeats
desc:
Given two integer arrays a and b, return the elements they have in common, counting repeats: a value that appears x times in a and y times in b must appear min(x, y) times in the result.

Return the result sorted in ascending order. If nothing is shared, return an empty array.

For example, a = [4, 9, 5, 9] and b = [9, 4, 9, 8, 4] give [4, 9, 9].
hints: Plain sets lose the repeat counts. What structure remembers how many times each value occurred?
Count the values of one array, then walk through the other array and consume from those counts.
Whenever the current value of b still has a positive remaining count, output it and decrement the count. Sort the output at the end.
editorial: Build a frequency map of a. Then scan b: if the map still holds a positive count for the current value, append the value to the result and decrement the count. Each shared copy is matched exactly once, so the number of copies kept per value is min(count in a, count in b). Sort the result to produce the canonical order.
Alternatively sort both arrays and walk them with two pointers, advancing the smaller side and emitting on equality. That needs no hash map and produces sorted output for free, at O(n log n) time.

title: Shortest Subarray with Same Degree
desc:
The degree of an array is the highest number of times any single value occurs in it. For example, the degree of [1, 3, 3, 2, 3, 1] is 3, because the value 3 occurs three times.

Given a non-empty integer array nums, find the shortest contiguous subarray whose degree equals the degree of the whole array, and return its length.
hints: Compute the degree first. Which values reach that frequency?
A shortest valid subarray can always be trimmed so that it starts and ends on an occurrence of a most frequent value.
Record the first index, last index and count of every value in one pass. For each value whose count equals the degree, candidate length is last - first + 1; take the minimum.
editorial: Any subarray with degree equal to the global degree d must contain some value v exactly d times, where v is one of the globally most frequent values. The shortest such window for a fixed v runs from its first occurrence to its last occurrence.
So one pass recording first[v], last[v] and count[v] is enough. The answer is the minimum of last[v] - first[v] + 1 over all values with count[v] equal to the maximum count. The runtime is linear.

title: Rotate Array by K Steps
desc:
Rotate the array nums to the right by k steps and return the rotated array. One step moves the last element to the front and shifts everything else one place to the right.

k can be far larger than the length of the array. Try to do the rotation with O(1) extra space besides the returned array (reversals make this possible).

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], k = 3
result = [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]
hints: Rotating by n steps gives back the same array. So only k mod n matters.
Look at the target: the last k elements move to the front, in their original order, followed by the first n - k elements.
Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n - k elements.
editorial: Reduce k to k mod n first, since a full turn changes nothing. After that, the rotated array is the last k elements followed by the first n - k elements.

Slicing builds this directly in O(n) extra space. To avoid the extra space, use three reversals: reversing the whole array puts the last k elements at the front but backwards, and the first n - k elements at the back but backwards. Reversing each of the two blocks again restores their order. Every element is swapped a constant number of times, so the time is O(n).
Simulating one step at a time costs O(n * k), which is far too slow once k reaches the billions.
solution:
def rotateArray(nums, k):
    a = list(nums)
    n = len(a)
    k %= n

    def rev(i, j):
        while i < j:
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
            i += 1
            j -= 1

    rev(0, n - 1)
    rev(0, k - 1)
    rev(k, n - 1)
    return a

title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays
desc:
Both a and b are sorted in non-decreasing order. Return a single array that contains every element of both arrays (duplicates included), also sorted in non-decreasing order.

Do it in O(n + m) time by using the fact that the inputs are already sorted, rather than sorting the combined array from scratch.

a = [1, 4, 4, 9], b = [2, 4, 10]
result = [1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 9, 10]
constraints: a and b are each sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: The smallest element overall must be the first element of a or the first element of b.
Keep one pointer in each array and repeatedly take the smaller of the two current elements.
When one array runs out, append everything that remains in the other one. Take from a on ties; either choice gives the same values.
editorial: This is the merge step of merge sort. Maintain indices i and j into the two arrays. While both are in range, compare a[i] and b[j], append the smaller one to the result, and advance that pointer. When one array is exhausted, copy over the rest of the other.

Each element is appended exactly once, so the running time is O(n + m). The result needs O(n + m) space because it has to be returned. Concatenating and calling a sort also works but costs O(n log n) and ignores the sortedness.

title: Range Sum Queries
desc:
You are given an integer array nums and a list of queries. Each query is a pair [l, r] asking for the sum of nums[l] + nums[l+1] + ... + nums[r] (both ends included, 0-indexed).

Return an array containing the answer to every query, in the same order as the queries. Many queries can be asked about the same array, so recomputing each sum from scratch is too slow.

nums = [3, -1, 4, 1, 5], queries = [[0, 2], [1, 1], [2, 4]]
result = [6, -1, 10]
constraints: 0 ≤ l ≤ r < nums.length for every query
hints: Summing each range directly costs O(n) per query, so O(n * q) overall. Can you share work between queries?
Build an array pre where pre[i] is the sum of the first i elements, with pre[0] = 0.
The sum of nums[l..r] equals pre[r + 1] - pre[l].
editorial: Precompute prefix sums once: pre[0] = 0 and pre[i + 1] = pre[i] + nums[i]. The sum of the elements from l to r inclusive is everything up to r minus everything before l, that is pre[r + 1] - pre[l].

Building the table takes O(n) and each query is answered in O(1), so the total is O(n + q). The leading zero in pre avoids a special case when l = 0. With the given bounds every sum has absolute value at most 108, comfortably inside 32 bits.

title: Squares of a Sorted Array
desc:
The array nums is sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain negative numbers. Build and return a new array holding the square of every element, also sorted in non-decreasing order.

Squaring and then sorting is easy to write. Can you take advantage of the fact that the input is already sorted and finish in O(n) time?

nums = [-4, -1, 0, 3, 10]
result = [0, 1, 9, 16, 100]
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: After squaring, the order is no longer sorted, because large negative numbers become large positive ones.
The largest square is always at one of the two ends of the input: either the most negative or the most positive value.
Keep a pointer at each end, compare absolute values, and fill the result array from the back with the larger square.
editorial: The squares of a sorted array form a valley shape: they shrink while the values are negative and grow again once they are positive. The biggest square therefore sits at the left end or the right end of the input.

Place one pointer at each end and fill the output from the last position down to the first. At each step compare abs(nums[lo]) and abs(nums[hi]), write the larger square, and move that pointer inward. Every element is handled once, so the time is O(n) with O(n) for the output. Sorting the squares directly costs O(n log n).

title: Maximum Sum of a Fixed Window
desc:
Given an integer array nums and a window length k, look at every contiguous block of exactly k elements and return the largest sum found among them.

nums = [1, 12, -5, -6, 50, 3], k = 4
windows: 2, 51, 42  (sums of [1,12,-5,-6], [12,-5,-6,50], [-5,-6,50,3])
result = 51
hints: Adding up each window from scratch costs O(n * k). Consecutive windows overlap almost completely.
Moving the window one step to the right removes exactly one element on the left and adds one on the right.
Compute the first window's sum once, then update it with sum += nums[i] - nums[i - k] while tracking the maximum.
editorial: Keep a running sum of the current window. Sliding the window by one position changes the sum by adding the new element at the right edge and subtracting the element that just fell off the left edge, which is O(1) per step.

Start with the sum of the first k elements as the best value, then slide through the rest of the array and keep the maximum. Total time is O(n) with O(1) extra space. Be careful to initialise the best value from a real window rather than from 0, since all sums can be negative.

title: Common Elements of Two Sorted Arrays
desc:
Two integer arrays a and b are each sorted in non-decreasing order. Return a sorted array containing every value they share, counting duplicates: a value that appears x times in a and y times in b must appear min(x, y) times in the result.

a = [1, 2, 2, 3, 5]
b = [2, 2, 2, 5, 7]
result = [2, 2, 5]
constraints: Both arrays are sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Counting values with a hash map works, but it ignores the fact that both arrays are sorted.
Use one pointer per array. Compare the two current values and decide which pointer can safely move.
If the values are equal, record one copy and advance both pointers; otherwise advance the pointer at the smaller value.
editorial: Because both arrays are sorted, a pointer into each array can sweep forward and never needs to go back. At each step compare a[i] and b[j]. The smaller one cannot match anything remaining in the other array (everything there is at least as large), so skip it. When they are equal, output the value and advance both pointers, which automatically pairs up duplicates the right number of times.

The loop does at most len(a) + len(b) steps, so the time is O(n + m) and extra space beyond the output is O(1). A hash-map approach is also O(n + m) but needs extra memory and loses the sorted order for free.

title: Count Negatives in a Sorted Grid
desc:
In the m x n integer matrix grid, every row is sorted in non-increasing order from left to right, and every column is sorted in non-increasing order from top to bottom.

Return how many cells of grid hold a negative number. A solution that visits far fewer than m * n cells exists.
constraints: Each row and each column is in non-increasing order
hints: Counting cell by cell works in O(m * n). Can the ordering let you skip many cells at once?
In one row, the negative numbers form a suffix. Binary searching each row for the first negative gives O(m log n).
Because columns are sorted too, the boundary between non-negatives and negatives only moves left as you go down. Walk it from the top-right corner and you only need O(m + n) steps.
editorial: Inside one row the values are non-increasing, so the negatives are exactly a suffix. A binary search for the first negative value counts a whole row in O(log n), for O(m log n) overall.

The columns are sorted as well, so the index of the first negative cell never moves right when you go to the next row down. Start at the top-right corner. While the current cell is negative, the whole column below it is negative too, so add the remaining rows and step left; otherwise step down. Each step either leaves a column or a row, so at most m + n steps are made: O(m + n) time and O(1) space.

title: Complete Staircase Rows
desc:
You have n coins and want to lay them out as a staircase. Row 1 takes one coin, row 2 takes two coins, row 3 takes three, and so on; row k takes k coins. A row is only counted if it is filled completely.

Return the number of complete rows you can build with the n coins.
hints: Building k complete rows costs exactly 1 + 2 + ... + k coins. Do you know a closed form for that sum?
The cost k(k+1)/2 grows with k, so the question "can I afford k rows?" is true for small k and false for large k.
Binary search the largest k with k(k+1)/2 ≤ n. The answer is below 65,536 for every allowed n, so use hi = 65,536; take care that intermediate products do not overflow 32 bits.
editorial: Subtracting 1, 2, 3, ... from n until the next row no longer fits is correct but needs about √(2n) steps, around 65,000 for the largest input. That is fine here, but binary search makes it logarithmic and generalizes to much larger limits.

Row counts are monotone: if k rows are affordable then so are k - 1. Search the largest k in [0, 65535] such that k(k+1)/2 ≤ n. Since k(k+1) can reach about 4.3 billion, do the arithmetic in a 64-bit type (or compare k(k+1)/2 carefully) in languages with 32-bit integers. The closed form floor((sqrt(8n + 1) - 1) / 2) also works but needs a careful integer square root.

title: Minimum Insertions to Balance Brackets
desc:
A string s consists only of the characters '(' and ')'. A bracket string is balanced when every '(' can be paired with a later ')' and every ')' with an earlier '(', with each bracket used in exactly one pair.

You may insert new brackets at any positions. Return the minimum number of insertions needed to make s balanced.
hints: Scan from left to right and keep track of the brackets that are still waiting for a partner.
A ')' that finds no waiting '(' can never be fixed by anything on its left, so it needs one inserted '(' right away.
Keep a counter of unmatched '(' and a counter of insertions. The answer is the insertions plus whatever unmatched '(' are left at the end.
editorial: Treat the string like a stack that only ever holds '(', so a single counter open is enough. For each '(' increase open. For each ')', if open > 0 it cancels one waiting bracket, otherwise it has no partner and we must insert a '(' (count one insertion).

After the scan every remaining waiting '(' needs one inserted ')', so the answer is insertions + open. Each insertion fixes exactly one unmatched bracket and the greedy decisions are forced, so the count is minimal. Time is O(n) with O(1) extra space.

title: Final Prices With a Special Discount
desc:
The array prices lists the prices of items in a shop, in the order they sit on a shelf. When you buy item i, you get a discount equal to the price of the first item j to its right (j > i) whose price satisfies prices[j] ≤ prices[i]. If no such item exists, you get no discount.

Return an array answer where answer[i] is the price you actually pay for item i.
hints: Checking every later item for every item is O(n<sup>2</sup>). For each item you only need the first later item that is not more expensive.
Walk left to right. An item that has not yet found its discount is waiting for a price that is at most its own.
Keep the waiting items on a stack of indices. When a new price arrives, pop every waiting item whose price is at least the new price and apply the discount to it; then push the new index.
editorial: This is a next smaller or equal element problem. Process the array left to right with a stack holding the indices of items that have not found a discount yet. The prices on the stack are always non-decreasing from bottom to top, because anything bigger than the incoming price gets popped.

For the incoming index i, while the item on top of the stack has price ≥ prices[i], pop it and subtract prices[i] from its final price: i is the first item to the right of it with a price that is not larger. Then push i. Every index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total time is O(n).

title: String Rotation Check
desc:
A rotation of a string moves some number of characters (possibly zero) from its front to its back, keeping their order. For example, rotating "abcde" by two gives "cdeab".

Given strings s and t, return true if t is a rotation of s, otherwise false. The two strings may have different lengths, in which case the answer is false.

For example, "abcde" and "cdeab" give true; "abcde" and "abced" give false; "aab" and "aba" give true.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase letters and digits
hints: Trying every rotation of s and comparing it with t works, but costs O(n²) for long strings. If the lengths differ you can answer immediately.
Write s twice in a row, for example "abcde" becomes "abcdeabcde". Where do the rotations of s show up in that doubled string?
Every rotation of s is a substring of length n of s + s, and nothing else of that length is. So after checking the lengths, ask whether t occurs inside s + s.
editorial: If the lengths differ, the answer is false. Otherwise, a rotation by k turns s = XY into YX, where X is the first k characters. The doubled string s + s = XYXY contains YX starting at position k, and the n-length windows of s + s are exactly the n rotations of s. So t is a rotation of s if and only if the lengths are equal and t occurs in s + s.

A naive substring search could cost O(n²) on repetitive input, so for a guaranteed linear bound use KMP or the Z-function on t + '#' + s + s. Modern built-in substring search is also fast in practice. Comparing all n rotations one by one is the O(n²) baseline.

title: Add Binary Strings
desc:
The strings a and b each hold a non-negative integer written in binary. Return their sum, also as a binary string.

The result must not have leading zeros unless it is exactly "0". The inputs can be far longer than any built-in integer type, so do the addition yourself, digit by digit.

For example, "11" + "1" gives "100", and "1010" + "1011" gives "10101".
constraints: a and b contain only the characters 0 and 1
Neither string has leading zeros, except for the string "0" itself
hints: Add the way you do on paper: start from the rightmost digits and move left, remembering a carry.
At every position the digit sum is bitA + bitB + carry, which is between 0 and 3. The new digit is that sum modulo 2, and the new carry is the sum divided by 2.
Keep going while either string has digits left or the carry is non-zero. Collect the digits in a list and reverse it at the end instead of prepending to a string.
editorial: Use two pointers starting at the last character of each string and a carry initialised to 0. In each step add the current digit of each string (treating an exhausted string as 0) plus the carry. Append sum % 2 to the output and set carry = sum // 2. When both strings are exhausted and the carry is zero, reverse the collected digits to get the answer.

Because both inputs have no leading zeros, the result never has them either, except that "0"+"0" yields a single "0". Converting to integers and back is not allowed in spirit here: the point is the digit-by-digit procedure, which runs in O(max(n, m)) time and works for numbers of any size.
solution:
def addBinary(a, b):
    i, j = len(a) - 1, len(b) - 1
    carry = 0
    out = []
    while i >= 0 or j >= 0 or carry:
        total = carry
        if i >= 0:
            total += ord(a[i]) - 48
            i -= 1
        if j >= 0:
            total += ord(b[j]) - 48
            j -= 1
        out.append(chr(48 + total % 2))
        carry = total // 2
    out.reverse()
    return "".join(out) if out else "0"

title: Roman Numeral to Integer
desc:
Roman numerals use seven symbols, written here in lowercase: i=1, v=5, x=10, l=50, c=100, d=500, m=1000.

Symbols are normally written from largest to smallest, left to right, and their values are added. There are six exceptions where a smaller symbol sits in front of a larger one and is subtracted: iv=4, ix=9, xl=40, xc=90, cd=400, cm=900.

Given a valid numeral s in this standard form, return the integer it represents. For example, "iii" is 3, "lviii" is 58 and "mcmxciv" is 1994.
constraints: s is a valid Roman numeral in standard form, representing an integer from 1 to 3999
s contains only the lowercase symbols i, v, x, l, c, d, m
hints: Adding the value of every symbol gets most numerals right. It fails only for the subtractive pairs such as iv and cm.
A symbol should be subtracted exactly when the symbol after it is worth more.
Scan left to right; for each position, add its value, unless the next symbol has a larger value, in which case subtract it.
editorial: Map each symbol to its value. Walk through the string: if the value at position i is smaller than the value at position i+1, it is the small half of a subtractive pair, so subtract it; otherwise add it. For "mcmxciv" this computes 1000 - 100 + 1000 - 10 + 100 - 1 + 5 = 1994.

An equivalent view scans right to left, keeping the previous value, and subtracts the current value whenever it is smaller than the one to its right. Either way the string is read once, giving O(n) time and O(1) space (the lookup table has seven entries).

title: First Occurrence of a Needle
desc:
Given two strings haystack and needle, return the smallest index i such that needle appears in haystack starting at position i. If needle does not occur in haystack, return -1.

For example, needle = "aba" first occurs in haystack = "ccababa" at index 2, while needle = "abc" does not occur in "ababab", so the answer is -1.

Implement the search yourself; a solution that runs in O(n + m) time is possible.
constraints: Both strings consist of lowercase English letters
needle may be longer than haystack, in which case the answer is -1
hints: Trying every start position and comparing character by character works, but it can take O(n · m) time on strings like "aaaa...a".

When a partial match fails, the characters you already matched tell you which later start positions are still possible. Precompute, for every prefix of the needle, the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix.

Build that table (the KMP failure function) for needle, then scan haystack once while keeping the current matched length; on a mismatch fall back with the table instead of moving the haystack pointer backwards.
editorial: The naive method aligns the needle at each position and compares until a mismatch. On inputs such as a haystack of 20,000 letters a and a needle of 10,000 as followed by a b, it repeats almost the whole comparison at every shift, which is O(n · m).

The Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm removes that waste. For each prefix of the needle, pi[i] stores the length of the longest proper prefix of needle[0..i] that is also its suffix. While scanning the haystack, keep k, the number of needle characters currently matched. On a mismatch, set k = pi[k-1] until the characters agree or k is zero; on a match, increase k. When k reaches the needle length the match started at i - m + 1.

Every step either increases k by one or decreases it, and k never goes below zero, so the total number of fallback steps is bounded by the number of increases. Building the table and scanning together take O(n + m) time and O(m) space.

title: Count Overlapping Occurrences
desc:
Count how many positions of text start a copy of pattern. Occurrences are allowed to overlap.

For example, pattern = "aa" occurs 3 times in text = "aaaa" (at positions 0, 1 and 2), and pattern = "aba" occurs 2 times in "ababa". If the pattern is longer than the text the answer is 0.
constraints: Both strings consist of lowercase English letters
hints: Checking every start position with a direct comparison is correct. Think about when that becomes slow.
After a full match you do not need to restart from scratch: the end of the match may already be the beginning of the next one.
Use the prefix function (failure table) of the pattern. When the matched length reaches the pattern length, count one occurrence and fall back to pi[len - 1] instead of resetting to 0.
editorial: Compute the prefix function pi of the pattern: pi[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. Then scan the text with a matched length k exactly as in KMP search.

The only change compared with finding the first occurrence is what happens on a full match. Instead of stopping, increment the counter and set k = pi[m - 1]. That value is the length of the longest border of the pattern, so it keeps exactly the characters that can also start the next, overlapping, occurrence.
Running time is O(n + m) and the extra memory is the O(m) table. Skipping past each match (restarting at i + m) would be a bug: it counts non-overlapping occurrences only.

title: Smallest Repeating Unit Length
desc:
A string s is built from a unit u if s equals u written one or more times in a row. Every string is built from itself, so a unit always exists. Return the length of the shortest unit of s.

For example, "abcabcabc" has shortest unit "abc" (length 3); "aaaa" has length 1; "abaab" has no smaller unit than itself, so the answer is 5.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: The unit length must divide s.length. How many candidate lengths is that, and how can you test one?
A string of length n has period p if s[i] == s[i + p] for all valid i. The unit must also be a period, and the string must split evenly.
Compute the prefix function. The smallest period of the whole string is n - pi[n-1]; it is a unit length exactly when it divides n, otherwise the answer is n.
editorial: Testing every divisor d of n by comparing s with s[:d] repeated works and is fast enough here, but a single linear pass is possible.

Let b = pi[n-1] be the length of the longest proper border of s (a prefix that is also a suffix). Then s has smallest period p = n - b. If p divides n, the string is exactly n / p copies of its first p characters, and no shorter unit exists because any unit length is also a period and p is the smallest one.

If p does not divide n, the string only repeats its prefix a fractional number of times. Then any unit would have to be a period that divides n; one smaller than n would force the smallest period to divide n as well (a consequence of the periodicity lemma), which it does not. So the answer is n. Time O(n), space O(n).

title: Tribonacci Modulo
desc:
The tribonacci sequence starts with T(0) = 0, T(1) = 1, T(2) = 1, and every later term is the sum of the three terms before it: T(k) = T(k-1) + T(k-2) + T(k-3).

Given n, return T(n) modulo 1,000,000,007. The terms grow exponentially, so the exact value quickly stops fitting in 32 bits.
hints: Write out the first ten terms by hand. Each one needs only the three terms right before it.
A plain recursion recomputes the same terms again and again. Compute the terms in increasing order instead, so each is calculated once.
Keep just three variables for the last three terms, and reduce modulo 1,000,000,007 after every addition so the numbers stay small.
editorial: The recurrence only looks back three positions, so a bottom-up loop with three rolling variables is enough. Start with (a, b, c) = (T(0), T(1), T(2)) and repeat (a, b, c) = (b, c, (a + b + c) mod M) until the window has moved n steps; then a holds T(n).

Taking the remainder at every step is valid because addition respects modular arithmetic. Each sum of three reduced terms stays below 3 × 10<sup>9</sup>, which overflows a signed 32-bit integer, so in such languages use a 64-bit type or reduce after each pairwise addition. The loop is O(n) time and O(1) space; matrix exponentiation would give O(log n) but is unnecessary here.

title: Staircase With Broken Steps
desc:
You stand on the ground (step 0) of a staircase whose top is step n. Each move climbs either 1 or 2 steps. Some steps listed in broken have collapsed, and you may never land on them (you can, however, jump over a single broken step).

Return the number of different sequences of moves that take you exactly to step n, modulo 1,000,000,007. If step n itself is broken the answer is 0.
constraints: 1 ≤ broken[i] ≤ n and all values are distinct (the array is not necessarily sorted)
hints: Think about the very last move. From which steps can you arrive at step i?
Let ways(i) be the number of ways to be standing on step i. Then ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2), except that ways(i) = 0 when step i is broken.
Mark the broken steps in a boolean array (or a set) and fill ways from 0 up to n, taking the remainder each time. Only the previous two values are needed.
editorial: This is the classic staircase recurrence with one twist. Let ways(0) = 1. For each step i from 1 to n, if step i is broken then ways(i) = 0; otherwise ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2) (treat negative indices as 0). Because a broken step has zero ways to be stood on, it contributes nothing to later steps, which exactly models never landing on it.

Reduce modulo 1,000,000,007 on every addition. Put the broken steps into a set (or a boolean array) first so each lookup is O(1). The total work is O(n + b) time with O(b) memory for the set and O(1) for the rolling values.
solution:
def countStaircaseWays(n, broken):
    M = 1000000007
    bad = set(broken)
    prev2, prev1 = 0, 1          # ways(-1), ways(0)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        cur = 0 if i in bad else (prev1 + prev2) % M
        prev2, prev1 = prev1, cur
    return prev1

title: Grid Paths with Obstacles
desc:
You are given a rectangular grid where 0 marks a free cell and 1 marks a blocked cell. A traveller starts in the top-left cell and wants to reach the bottom-right cell, moving only one step right or one step down at a time and never entering a blocked cell.

Return the number of different routes. If the start or the destination is blocked, the answer is 0. The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit signed integer.
constraints: The start and destination cells may themselves be blocked
hints: Think about the last step of any route. Which two neighbouring cells can the traveller come from?
Let ways[r][c] be the number of routes that end in cell (r, c). A blocked cell has ways = 0; a free cell gets ways[r-1][c] + ways[r][c-1].
Seed the start cell with 1 (unless it is blocked). Only the previous row is needed, so one array of width n can be updated in place.
editorial: Every route into a free cell arrives from the cell above or the cell on its left, and these two sets of routes are disjoint, so ways[r][c] = ways[r-1][c] + ways[r][c-1]. A blocked cell can never be stood on, so its count is forced to 0, which automatically prevents any route from passing through it.

Row r only reads row r-1 and the cell to its own left, so a single array of length n is enough: for each cell, set it to 0 if blocked, otherwise add the value of its left neighbour to the value it already holds from the row above. This runs in O(m · n) time and O(n) space. Because the closed-form binomial count no longer applies once obstacles appear, the DP is the natural tool.

title: Minimum Path Sum in a Grid
desc:
Every cell of the rectangular grid holds a non-negative toll. Starting in the top-left cell you must reach the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down. You pay the toll of every cell you stand on, including the first and the last one.

Return the smallest total toll over all possible routes.
hints: Greedily stepping to the cheaper neighbour can fail, because a cheap cell may lead into an expensive region. Consider the last cell of the route instead.
The cheapest route into cell (r, c) must come from above or from the left. Define best[r][c] as the cheapest toll to reach it.
best[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(best[r-1][c], best[r][c-1]); the first row and first column only have one possible predecessor.
editorial: Let best[r][c] be the minimum total toll of a route from the top-left cell to (r, c). The last step of that route came from (r-1, c) or (r, c-1), and the part before that step must itself be optimal, otherwise swapping in a cheaper prefix would improve the route. That gives best[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(best[r-1][c], best[r][c-1]).

On the first row there is no cell above and on the first column no cell to the left, so those cells simply extend the single available predecessor. Process cells row by row; a single array holding the current row of best values is sufficient. Time O(m · n), extra space O(n).

title: 0/1 Knapsack Maximum Value
desc:
A thief finds n distinct items. Item i weighs weights[i] and is worth values[i]. The bag can carry a total weight of at most capacity, and every item can be taken at most once (or left behind).

Return the largest total value that fits in the bag. Taking nothing is allowed, so the answer is never negative.
hints: Greedy by value-per-weight fails here, because items cannot be split. Think about deciding item by item: take it or skip it.
Let best[c] be the best value achievable with total weight at most c using the items seen so far. Adding an item of weight w and value v can turn best[c - w] into best[c - w] + v.
Update the one-dimensional array from the largest capacity down to the smallest, so that each item is used at most once. The answer is best[capacity].
editorial: Process the items one at a time. After handling some prefix of the items, let best[c] be the maximum value of a selection from that prefix whose total weight is at most c. Handling a new item of weight w and value v gives best[c] = max(best[c], best[c - w] + v) for every c ≥ w: either skip the item, or take it on top of the best selection for the smaller capacity.

The loop over c must run downward. Going downward guarantees that best[c - w] still describes the state before this item, so the item is counted once. Going upward would let the same item be reused, which turns this into the unbounded knapsack. The cost is O(n · capacity) time and O(capacity) space.

title: Unbounded Knapsack Maximum Value
desc:
A shop sells n kinds of items in unlimited quantity. One item of kind i weighs weights[i] and is worth values[i]. You may pack any number of copies of each kind (including none) as long as the total weight is at most capacity.

Return the maximum total value you can pack.
hints: Compared with the 0/1 version, an item can now be used again after you have used it. Which direction of loop allows that?
Let best[c] be the maximum value with total weight at most c. The last item placed has some weight w and value v, so best[c] = best[c - w] + v for some kind.
For every capacity c from 1 to capacity, and every kind, try best[c] = max(best[c], best[c - w] + v). Capacities increase, so best[c - w] may already include the same kind.
editorial: Let best[c] be the largest value achievable with total weight at most c, with best[0] = 0. If an optimal packing for capacity c is non-empty, remove one item of some kind i; what remains is a packing for capacity c - weights[i]. So best[c] is the maximum of best[c - 1] (leave one unit of capacity unused) and best[c - weights[i]] + values[i] over all kinds i that fit.

Iterating capacities upward means best[c - w] may already contain copies of the same kind, which is exactly what unlimited supply allows. This is the one-line difference from the 0/1 knapsack, where the capacity loop runs downward. Time is O(n · capacity) and space is O(capacity).

title: Longest Common Substring
desc:
Given two strings s and t, return the length of the longest string that appears in both of them as a contiguous block of characters (a substring, not merely a subsequence).

If the strings have no character in common, or one of them is empty, the answer is 0.

s = "xabcdy", t = "zzabcdq"  ->  4   ("abcd")
s = "abab",   t = "baba"     ->  3   ("aba" or "bab")
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Try every pair of starting positions and extend while the characters keep matching. That works, but it repeats a lot of comparisons. How could you reuse the work of a previous pair?
Let L(i, j) be the length of the longest common block that ends exactly at position i of s and position j of t. If the two characters differ, L(i, j) = 0; otherwise L(i, j) = L(i-1, j-1) + 1.
The answer is the maximum value of L(i, j) over all cells, not the last cell. Each row only needs the row above it, so two arrays of length t.length + 1 are enough.
editorial: Define L[i][j] as the length of the longest common substring that ends at s[i-1] and t[j-1]. A common block that ends at these two positions must either be empty (the characters differ) or be one character longer than the block ending at the previous pair of positions, so L[i][j] = L[i-1][j-1] + 1 when the characters match and 0 otherwise.

Unlike the subsequence version, a mismatch resets the run to zero instead of carrying the best value forward, because the block must stay contiguous. The answer is the largest value seen anywhere in the table. Keeping only the previous row gives O(t.length) memory. Comparing every pair of start positions and extending is O(m · n · min(m, n)) in the worst case, far too slow at the upper limits.

title: Make Two Strings Equal by Deleting
desc:
In one move you may delete a single character from either word1 or word2. Return the minimum number of moves needed to make the two strings identical.

Deleting everything from both strings always works, so an answer exists; two empty strings count as identical.

word1 = "sea",  word2 = "eat"   ->  2   (delete 's' and 't', both become "ea")
word1 = "abc",  word2 = "xyz"   ->  6
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Whatever strings remain after all deletions must be equal. What can you say about that remaining string in relation to word1 and to word2?
The remaining string is a subsequence of both words. To use as few deletions as possible, keep as many characters as possible.
If the longest common subsequence has length L, the answer is len(word1) + len(word2) - 2 * L. Compute L with the usual table over prefixes.
editorial: After the deletions the two strings are equal, so the surviving string is a common subsequence of both inputs. Every character of word1 outside it was deleted, as was every character of word2 outside it. If the survivor has length k, the number of deletions is (m - k) + (n - k), which is smallest when k is as large as possible. So the task is exactly to find the longest common subsequence.

Compute the LCS with dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 when word1[i-1] == word2[j-1] and max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) otherwise, keeping a single previous row to save memory. The answer is m + n - 2 * dp[m][n]. A direct search over which characters to delete is exponential.

title: Flood Fill Recolor
desc:
An image is a grid of integers where each cell holds a color. Starting at the cell (sr, sc), repaint that cell and every cell reachable from it by steps up, down, left or right that passes only through cells having the same color as the starting cell, using the new color color.

Return the repainted image. The cells that are not part of this connected same-colored region must be left unchanged.

image = [[1,1,0],
         [1,0,0],
         [1,1,1]],  sr = 0, sc = 0, color = 7

result = [[7,7,0],
          [7,0,0],
          [7,7,7]]
hints: Only the cells of the starting cell's original color that touch each other (through the four directions) are recolored.
Remember the original color first, then explore from the start with a stack or queue, moving only onto cells that still have that original color.

If the new color already equals the original color, the image does not change at all. Handle that case up front, otherwise recoloring cannot tell visited cells from unvisited ones and the search never ends.
editorial: Read the color old of the start cell. If old == color return a copy of the image straight away. Otherwise run a BFS or DFS from (sr, sc): paint a cell with the new color at the moment you push it, and only push neighbours whose current color is still old. Painting acts as the visited marker, which is why the early return for the equal-color case is needed.
Each cell is pushed at most once, so the time is O(rows × cols). Using an explicit stack avoids deep recursion on a 50 × 50 region.

title: Island Perimeter Length
desc:
In a grid, a 1 is a unit square of land and a 0 is water. Every land square has four sides. A side is part of the perimeter if the square next to it (above, below, left or right) is water, or if that side lies on the outer edge of the grid.

Return the total number of perimeter sides over all land squares. Water enclosed by land (a lake) also contributes its boundary sides, and the grid may hold any number of separate islands.

grid = [[0,1,0,0],
        [1,1,1,0],
        [0,1,0,0]]   -> 12
hints: You do not need to find islands at all. Think about each land square on its own.
A single land square contributes 4 sides. Two land squares that touch hide one side of each.
Count 4 per land square, then subtract 2 for every pair of land squares that are adjacent. Check only the cell above and the cell to the left so each pair is counted once.
editorial: Look at each land square independently: it has four sides, and each side is on the perimeter unless the neighbour across it is land. Equivalently, the answer is 4 * land - 2 * shared, where shared is the number of adjacent land pairs (each pair removes one side from both squares).

Scan the grid once. For every land cell add one to land and add one to shared for the land cell directly above it and for the one directly to its left. This is O(rows × cols) time and O(1) extra space, and it works for any number of islands and lakes because only local neighbours matter.

title: Star Graph Center
desc:
A star graph has one center node that is joined directly to every other node, and has no other connections. The graph has n nodes labelled 1 to n and therefore exactly n - 1 edges.

You are given the edges as pairs edges[i] = [a, b], in no particular order and with either endpoint first. The edges are guaranteed to describe a star graph. Return the label of its center.
constraints: The edges form a valid star graph
hints: In a star every edge touches the center. What does that say about any two different edges?
Two different edges share exactly one node, and that shared node must be the center.
You only need the first two edges: whichever endpoint of edge 0 also appears in edge 1 is the answer. No counting is required.
editorial: Counting how often each label occurs works: the center occurs in every edge, so it is the one label with count n - 1. That takes O(n) time and O(n) space.

A constant-time observation does better. Because n ≥ 3 there are at least two edges, and both contain the center. Each of those edges has two endpoints; the center is the only label they have in common. So compare the endpoints of edges[0] with the endpoints of edges[1] and return the shared one. The other labels are leaves and each appears in just one edge, so they can never be shared.
solution:
def findCenter(edges):
    a, b = edges[0]
    c, d = edges[1]
    return a if a == c or a == d else b

title: Path Exists in an Undirected Graph
desc:
A network has n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1. Each entry edges[i] = [a, b] is a two-way connection between nodes a and b. No pair of nodes is joined by more than one edge and no node is joined to itself.

Return true if you can travel from node source to node destination by following connections, and false otherwise. A node can always reach itself.
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b, source, destination < n, and a ≠ b
No two edges join the same pair of nodes
hints: Think of the connections as a graph. The question is whether two nodes lie in the same connected piece.
Starting from source, repeatedly visit neighbours you have not seen yet (BFS or DFS) and note everything you reach.
Build an adjacency list first, keep a visited array, and stop early when you pop destination. Use an explicit queue or stack so a 2,000-node chain cannot overflow the recursion limit.
editorial: Turn the edge list into an adjacency list, adding each edge in both directions. Run a breadth-first search from source, marking nodes as visited when they are first put on the queue. If destination is ever reached the answer is true; if the queue empties first, it is false. When source and destination are the same node the search succeeds immediately.

A union-find structure is an equally good alternative: union the endpoints of every edge, then compare the representatives of the two nodes. It never builds an adjacency list and is handy if the question has to be answered for many pairs. Both approaches take O(n + m) time.

title: Maximum Depth of a Binary Tree
desc:
Given a binary tree, return its depth: the number of nodes on the longest path that starts at the root and ends at a leaf. The empty tree has depth 0.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [3, 9, 20, -1, -1, 15, 7] the answer is 3 (for example 3 → 20 → 15).
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Depth is a property you can compute for every node: how deep does the path to it go?
A child is exactly one level deeper than its parent. Walk the tree from the root and remember the largest level you see.
Recursively: depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)) with depth(missing) = 0. Or process the array level by level and count the levels.
editorial: The recursive definition is the cleanest: an empty tree has depth 0, otherwise the depth is one more than the larger depth of the two subtrees. Every node is visited once, so the running time is linear.

With the array encoding you can avoid recursion completely. The real nodes appear in level order, so the k-th real node's children sit at array slots 2k+1 and 2k+2. Parents always come before their children, so a single left-to-right pass can assign depth[child] = depth[parent] + 1 and track the maximum.

title: Subtree of Another Binary Tree
desc:
Given two binary trees tree and sub, decide whether sub occurs inside tree. It does if some node of tree, taken together with all of its descendants, forms a tree that is identical to sub in both shape and node values.

A node with only some of its descendants does not count, and the empty tree is considered to occur in every tree (including the empty one). Return true or false.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

Both arguments use this encoding. With tree = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2] and sub = [4, 1, 2] the answer is true. If node 2 of tree had an extra child, as in [3, 4, 5, 1, 2, -1, -1, -1, -1, 0], the answer would be false.
constraints: 0 ≤ number of nodes in each tree ≤ 1,500
Both arrays follow the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
