The one-pass dynamic-programming form is more compact. Let best be the minimum deletions to order the prefix seen so far, and b the number of b's seen. A new b can always be appended (just increment b). A new a either gets deleted (best + 1) or forces all earlier b's to be deleted (b), so best = min(best + 1, b).

title: Find First and Last Position of Target
desc:
Given an array nums sorted in non-decreasing order, find where the value target starts and ends. Return [first, last], the lowest and highest indices holding target. If target does not occur, return [-1, -1].

The solution must run in O(log n) time, so scanning outward from a match is not good enough when there are many duplicates.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: One binary search can find some index holding the target, but with many duplicates that index tells you little about the edges.
Run two binary searches that each look for a boundary: the first index with value ≥ target and the first index with value > target.
The range is [lower, upper - 1]. If lower == upper (or lower is out of bounds) the target is absent.
editorial: Define lowerBound(x) as the first index whose value is ≥ x, or n if none. The first occurrence of target is lowerBound(target) provided that index is in range and holds the target. The index after the last occurrence is lowerBound(target + 1), so the last occurrence is that minus one.

Both bounds come from the same binary search routine, so the total cost is two O(log n) searches. Be careful that target + 1 can exceed the 32-bit range in fixed-width languages; implementing an upper bound with a strict nums[mid] ≤ target test avoids that.

title: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days
desc:
A conveyor belt carries packages with the given weights, in the order they arrive. Each day the ship loads packages in that order, without reordering and without exceeding its weight capacity, then sails. A package cannot be split across days.

Return the smallest ship capacity that lets all packages be shipped within days days.
hints: Try a fixed capacity: how would you count the number of days it needs? Load greedily and start a new day when the next package no longer fits.
If a capacity works, any larger capacity works too, so feasibility is monotonic in the capacity.
Binary search the capacity between max(weights) (the heaviest single package must fit) and sum(weights) (ship everything in one day), using the greedy count as the test.
editorial: The capacity must be at least the heaviest package and is never worth more than the total weight. For a candidate capacity, simulate greedily: keep adding packages to the current day until the next one would overflow, then begin a new day. Greedy loading uses the fewest possible days for that capacity.

Since a larger capacity never needs more days, the predicate "fits within days" flips from false to true exactly once. Binary search the smallest capacity where it is true. There are about log(sum) iterations, each costing O(n), for O(n log(sum)) time and O(1) space.

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
desc: You are given a binary array nums (every element is 0 or 1) and an integer k. You may flip at most k zeros into ones. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive ones you can obtain.
hints: Instead of thinking about flipping, ask: what is the longest subarray that contains at most k zeros?
A window with too many zeros can be repaired by shrinking it from the left; a valid window can be extended on the right.
Expand right one step at a time, counting zeros. While the count exceeds k, move left forward (decrementing the count if the dropped element was a zero). Track the largest window.
editorial: Flipping at most k zeros inside a stretch is possible exactly when that stretch contains at most k zeros. So the answer is the length of the longest subarray with at most k zeros.

Use a sliding window. Add nums[right], and if it is a zero increase the zero count. If the count passes k, advance left until the count is back to k. After each step, the window [left, right] is valid, so update the best length. Each index enters and leaves the window at most once: O(n) time, O(1) space.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
desc:
Each interval is a pair [start, end] with start < end. Two intervals overlap when they share more than a single point, so intervals that merely touch, such as [1, 2] and [2, 3], do not overlap.

Return the minimum number of intervals you have to remove so that the remaining intervals are pairwise non-overlapping.
hints: Removing the fewest intervals is the same as keeping the largest possible set of mutually compatible intervals.
When choosing which interval to keep first, the one that finishes earliest leaves the most room for the rest.
Sort by end value. Sweep through, keeping an interval whenever its start is at least the end of the last kept interval; otherwise count it as removed.
editorial: This is the classic activity-selection problem. Maximise the number of intervals kept; the answer is n - kept.

Greedy rule: sort by end and always keep the interval that ends first among those compatible with what you already kept. An exchange argument shows this is optimal: any optimal solution can swap its first interval for the earliest-ending one without creating a conflict. Sorting costs O(n log n) and the sweep is O(n); extra space is for the sorted copy.

title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
desc:
Balloons are pinned to a wall. Balloon i covers the horizontal range [points[i][0], points[i][1]] (both ends included). An arrow shot straight up from position x bursts every balloon whose range contains x, and the arrow keeps going.

Return the minimum number of arrows needed to burst all balloons.
hints: Balloons whose ranges share a common point can be burst by a single arrow.
Sort the balloons by their right end. Shooting at the right end of the first balloon is never worse than shooting anywhere else inside it.
Shoot at the current right end; every following balloon whose left end is ≤ that position is already burst. The first balloon whose left end is larger needs a new arrow, placed at its own right end.
editorial: Sort balloons by right end. Place the first arrow at the right end of the first balloon: any arrow that bursts that balloon can be slid right to its end without losing any other balloon that is later in the sorted order, so this position is at least as good as any other.

Walk through the sorted list. A balloon with start ≤ arrowPos is already burst. Otherwise fire a new arrow at its right end and continue. Since both ends are inclusive, a balloon that starts exactly at the arrow position is hit. Comparisons only (no sums) keep the logic safe at the 32-bit limits. O(n log n) for sorting, O(1) beyond that.

title: Car Fleet
desc:
Several cars drive along a one-lane road towards a destination at mile target. Car i starts at mile position[i] and moves at a constant speed[i] miles per hour. All starting positions are distinct and lie before the destination.

A car can never pass the car in front of it. If it catches up, it slows down and from then on travels at the speed of that car, bumper to bumper; together they form a fleet. A single car is also a fleet, and a car that catches up exactly at the destination still joins the fleet that arrives there.

Return the number of fleets that arrive at the destination.
constraints: 0 ≤ position[i] < target, and all positions are distinct
hints: Process the cars from the one closest to the destination backwards. A car's fate depends only on the cars in front of it.
For each car compute the time it would need if the road were empty: (target - position) / speed. A car with a time not larger than the fleet ahead of it will merge into that fleet.

Go in descending order of position and keep the arrival time of the fleet in front (a stack, or just its top). A car whose time is strictly larger starts a new fleet. Compare fractions by cross-multiplying to avoid rounding.
editorial: Sort cars by starting position, nearest to the destination first. The first car is always the head of a fleet. For each next car, compute its free-road arrival time t = (target - p) / s. If t is not larger than the arrival time of the fleet immediately ahead, it catches up (or ties exactly at the finish) and joins it; its effective time becomes the fleet's time. If t is strictly larger, it will never catch that fleet and becomes the head of a new one.

Only the time of the closest fleet ahead matters, which is the top of a monotonic stack of fleet times (strictly increasing from the front car backwards). To stay exact, compare (target - p1) / s1 > (target - p2) / s2 as (target - p1) * s2 > (target - p2) * s1; the products are at most 1012, which needs 64-bit arithmetic in some languages. Sorting dominates: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
solution:
def carFleet(target, position, speed):
    cars = sorted(zip(position, speed), reverse=True)
    fleets = 0
    lead_dist = lead_speed = None
    for p, s in cars:
        d = target - p
        # strictly later than the fleet ahead: d / s > lead_dist / lead_speed
        if lead_dist is None or d * lead_speed > lead_dist * s:
            fleets += 1
            lead_dist, lead_speed = d, s
    return fleets

title: Gas Station
desc:
There are n gas stations arranged in a circle. Station i sells gas[i] units of fuel, and driving from station i to the next station (i + 1) % n burns cost[i] units.

You begin at some station with an empty tank, fill up there, and then drive clockwise, refuelling at every station you reach. You complete the circuit if the tank never goes below zero on the way and you arrive back at the starting station. Return the smallest starting index from which you can complete the circuit, or -1 if no start works.
hints: Trying every start and simulating the lap costs O(n²). Look for structure that lets you skip many starts at once.
If the total gas is smaller than the total cost, the answer is -1 straight away. Otherwise some start works.
Sweep once, keeping a running tank. When the tank drops below zero at station i, none of the starts between the previous candidate and i can work, so restart the candidate at i + 1.
editorial: If sum(gas) < sum(cost), no start works. Otherwise a valid start exists, and a single sweep finds it. Keep a running tank from a candidate start. If the tank becomes negative after station i, then starting at any station between the candidate and i would have reached i with at most as much fuel, and would fail too. So the next candidate is i + 1 and the tank resets.

The candidate left at the end of the sweep is the answer. It is also the smallest valid index, because it is the first position where the prefix sum of gas[i] - cost[i] reaches its global minimum. The sweep is O(n) time with O(1) extra space.

title: Jump Game II
desc:
You stand on index 0 of the integer array nums. From index i you may jump forward by any distance from 1 to nums[i] (so a value of 0 means you cannot move from there).

Return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index. The input is built so that the last index is always reachable.
constraints: The last index is reachable from index 0
hints: A DP where dp[i] is the fewest jumps to reach i works, but is O(n²) in the worst case.
Think of the indices reachable with 1 jump, then with 2 jumps, and so on. Each group is a contiguous range, like levels of a BFS.
Track the end of the current range and the farthest index reachable from anything inside it. When you pass the end of the range, take a jump and extend the range to the farthest point.
editorial: Treat the array as an implicit graph and run BFS, noticing that the set of indices reachable in exactly k jumps forms a contiguous block. Keep cur_end, the last index reachable with the jumps taken so far, and far, the farthest index reachable by one more jump from any index seen so far.

Scan from left to right, updating far = max(far, i + nums[i]). When i reaches cur_end you must jump again: increment the counter and set cur_end = far. Stop the scan before the last index. This greedy is O(n) time and O(1) space.

title: Spiral Matrix
desc: Given an m x n integer matrix, return all of its elements in a single flat array, reading them in clockwise spiral order: start at the top-left cell, go right along the top row, then down the right column, then left along the bottom row, then up the left column, and keep spiralling inwards until every cell has been visited once.
constraints: Every row has exactly n elements
hints: Picture four edges of a rectangle that you peel off one at a time. How do the edges change after each full loop?
Maintain four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right. After walking along an edge, move that boundary one step inwards.
Be careful when only one row or one column is left: after walking the top row and the right column, check that top ≤ bottom and left ≤ right before walking back, or you will read cells twice.
editorial: Keep four indices top, bottom, left, right bounding the unvisited rectangle. Repeat while top ≤ bottom and left ≤ right: read the top row left to right and increment top; read the right column top to bottom and decrement right; if rows remain, read the bottom row right to left and decrement bottom; if columns remain, read the left column bottom to top and increment left.

The two guards before the last two edges handle matrices that collapse to a single row or column in the middle of the walk. Each cell is appended once, so the running time is O(m * n) and the extra space beyond the output is O(1). An alternative is to simulate the walk with a visited grid and turn right whenever the next cell is blocked.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
desc:
Given an m x n integer matrix, whenever a cell contains 0, set every cell in its entire row and its entire column to 0. Return the resulting matrix.

All decisions are based on the original matrix: zeros created by this process must not cause further rows or columns to be cleared. Aim for O(1) extra space beyond the matrix itself.
hints: First collect the rows and columns that contain a zero in the original matrix, and only then start writing zeros.
Two arrays, one boolean per row and one per column, are enough. Can you store those flags inside the matrix itself?
Use the first row and first column as the flag storage. Remember separately whether the first row and the first column originally contained a zero, since they are overwritten by the markers.
editorial: The straightforward approach records which rows and which columns contain a zero in two arrays of size m and n, then does a second pass clearing every cell whose row or column is flagged. That uses O(m + n) extra space.

To get O(1) extra space, reuse the first row and first column as the flag arrays. Before anything else, note whether row 0 and column 0 contain a zero. Then scan the rest of the matrix and, on seeing a zero at (i, j), set matrix[i][0] and matrix[0][j] to 0. Next clear every cell (i, j) with i, j ≥ 1 whose row marker or column marker is 0. Finally clear the first row and first column if they were flagged at the start.

title: K Closest Points to Origin
desc:
You are given points, a list of [x, y] coordinates on a plane, and an integer k. Return the k points that are closest to the origin (0, 0) by straight-line (Euclidean) distance.

The points may be returned in any order. The input is built so that the set of k closest points is unique: when k < n, the k-th closest point is strictly closer than the (k+1)-th closest.
constraints: The answer set is unique (no tie at the boundary of the k-th and (k+1)-th closest)
hints: Sorting all points by distance and taking the first k works in O(n log n). You do not need the full order, though.
You can compare squared distances x*x + y*y, so no square root or floating point is needed.
Keep a max-heap of size k holding the best points seen so far, keyed by distance. If a new point is closer than the heap's top, replace the top.
editorial: Compare squared distances to avoid floating point arithmetic. The simplest solution sorts the points by squared distance and slices the first k, in O(n log n).

A heap does better when k is small: maintain a max-heap (keyed by squared distance) containing at most k points. For every new point, push it; if the heap grows beyond k, pop the farthest point. After scanning all points the heap holds the k closest, in O(n log k) time and O(k) space. Quickselect can reach O(n) on average.

title: Task Scheduler
desc:
A CPU must run every task in tasks, where equal numbers mean tasks of the same type. Each unit of time the CPU either runs one task or sits idle. The tasks may be executed in any order, but two tasks of the same type must be separated by at least n units of time (so after running a task of some type, the next task of that type may start no earlier than n + 1 time units later).

Return the minimum total number of time units needed to finish all the tasks, counting idle units.
hints: Only the number of tasks of each type matters, not their order in the input. Start by counting them.
Greedy idea: in each window of n + 1 time units, run the most frequent remaining types, one task of each distinct type.
Use a max-heap of remaining counts. In every round pop up to n + 1 types, run one task of each, push back those with tasks left, and add n + 1 to the time unless this was the final round.
editorial: Count the tasks of each type and put the counts in a max-heap. Time is processed in rounds of n + 1 units. In a round, pop up to n + 1 of the largest counts (each pop is a different type, so the cooldown is respected), decrement them, and remember those that still have work. After the round push them back. If the heap is non-empty the round consumed all n + 1 units (idle slots included); in the final round only as many units as tasks were run are added.

Always running the types with the most remaining work is optimal because the most frequent type is the bottleneck. There is also a closed form: with m the largest count and c the number of types having that count, the answer is max(len(tasks), (m - 1) * (n + 1) + c).
solution:
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def leastInterval(tasks, n):
    heap = [-c for c in Counter(tasks).values()]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    time = 0
    while heap:
        slots = n + 1
        left = []
        while slots and heap:
            c = heapq.heappop(heap) + 1
            slots -= 1
            if c < 0:
                left.append(c)
        for c in left:
            heapq.heappush(heap, c)
        time += (n + 1) if heap else (n + 1 - slots)
    return time

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
desc:
Given an array nums of positive integers, decide whether it can be split into two groups (every element goes into exactly one group) such that both groups have the same sum.

Return true if such a split exists and false otherwise.
hints: If the total is odd, the answer is immediately no. Otherwise each group must sum to half of the total.
The question becomes: is there a subset of the numbers that adds up to total / 2? Think of a 0/1 knapsack.
Keep a boolean array reach[s] meaning 'some subset sums to s'. For each number x, update sums from high to low: reach[s] |= reach[s - x].
editorial: The two groups sum to the total, so each must sum to total / 2; an odd total makes it impossible. Finding one group with sum target = total / 2 automatically leaves the rest with the same sum.

This is subset-sum. Let reach[s] be true when some subset of the processed numbers adds to s, starting with only reach[0] true. For each number x iterate s from target down to x (downwards so x is used at most once) and set reach[s] |= reach[s - x]. The answer is reach[target]. The sum is at most 20,000, so this is about 200 × 10,000 steps. A big-integer bitmask (bits |= bits << x) performs the same update in one operation per number.

title: Number of Provinces
desc:
There are n cities. Some pairs of cities are directly linked by a road; two cities can also reach each other indirectly through a chain of roads. A province is a maximal group of cities that can all reach one another.

You are given an n x n matrix isConnected where isConnected[i][j] = 1 means city i and city j are directly linked and 0 means they are not. Every city is linked to itself.

Return the number of provinces.
hints: Cities form an undirected graph. A province is exactly one connected component.
Start a DFS or BFS from any city you have not visited, marking every city you can reach. Each start counts as a new province.
Alternatively use union-find: begin with n separate sets, merge the sets of i and j whenever they are linked, and subtract one from the count each time a merge actually joins two different sets.
editorial: Count connected components of the graph described by the matrix. With union-find, start with n components. For each pair i < j with isConnected[i][j] = 1, find the roots of i and j; if they differ, union them and decrease the component count by one. The final count is the answer.

Use path compression (and optionally union by size) so each find is near constant time. The matrix has n² entries, so reading it dominates: O(n² · α(n)). A DFS or BFS over the matrix rows gives the same bound.

title: Redundant Connection
desc:
A connected, cycle-free graph (a tree) on nodes 1..n had one extra edge added between two nodes that were not already directly connected. You are given the resulting list edges of n undirected edges; edges[i] = [a, b] joins nodes a and b.

Removing a suitable edge turns the graph back into a tree. If several edges could be removed, return the one that appears last in edges. Return it exactly as written in the input (same order of its two numbers).
constraints: edges[i] = [a, b] with 1 ≤ a, b ≤ n and a ≠ b
No two edges join the same pair of nodes
hints: Adding one edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle. The answer lies on that cycle.
Process the edges in order, keeping track of which nodes are already connected. When would an edge be redundant?
Use union-find: for each edge, if both endpoints already share a root, this edge closes the cycle and is the answer; otherwise union them.
editorial: Insert the edges one by one into a union-find structure. For an edge [a, b], find the roots of a and b. If the roots differ, the edge connects two separate pieces, so union them. If the roots are equal, a and b were already connected by earlier edges, so this edge completes the unique cycle.

That edge is also the last cycle edge in the input: every other edge of the single cycle came earlier (it was needed to connect a and b), and edges after it are not on the cycle. So the first edge found to be redundant while scanning in order is the required answer. With path compression this runs in nearly linear time.

title: Combination Sum II
desc:
Given an array candidates of positive integers (values may repeat) and a positive integer target, find every distinct combination of candidates whose sum is exactly target.

Each element of the array may be used at most once, but if a value appears several times in the array it may be picked up to that many times. Two combinations are the same if they contain the same values with the same multiplicities, regardless of which copies were chosen.

Return the combinations as rows with their numbers written in non-decreasing order. The rows can be listed in any order, and no combination may be listed twice. If no combination works, return an empty list.
hints: Sort the array so equal values sit next to each other and each row comes out in non-decreasing order.
Do a depth-first search where each step picks the next element to include, moving forward through the sorted array so no element is reused. Stop when the remaining sum is negative.
To avoid duplicate rows, at any one level of the recursion skip a value if it is equal to the previous value you already tried at that same level.
editorial: Sort the candidates. Recurse with a start index and the remaining target. In the loop over i from start, break as soon as candidates[i] exceeds the remaining target (all later values are at least as large). Otherwise take it, recurse with start i + 1 (each element is used once), and undo.

Duplicates are removed with one rule: inside a single loop, if i > start and candidates[i] == candidates[i - 1], skip it. The first copy of a value covers every combination that begins with that value at this position, while a later copy at the same level would repeat them. Copies of the same value are still allowed deeper in the recursion because there the index equals the start of the new loop.

title: Shortest Path in a Binary Matrix
desc:
You are given an n x n grid of 0s (open cells) and 1s (blocked cells). A clear path goes from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, visits only open cells, and moves between cells that touch either along a side or at a corner, so each step may go in any of the 8 directions.

The length of a path is the number of cells it visits, including the first and the last. Return the length of the shortest clear path, or -1 if there is none.
constraints: The start or the end cell may itself be blocked, in which case the answer is -1
hints: Every step costs the same, so which classic algorithm finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph?
Use breadth-first search from the top-left cell, expanding to all 8 neighbours that are in range and open. Don't forget to check that the start cell is open.
Mark a cell as visited when you push it on the queue, and keep the distance with it (or process the queue level by level). The first time you pop the bottom-right cell, its distance is the answer.
editorial: The grid is an unweighted graph where each open cell is connected to up to eight open neighbours, so BFS gives the shortest path. If the start or end cell is blocked, return -1 right away. Put the start in a queue with distance 1 and mark it visited. Pop a cell; if it is the bottom-right cell, return its distance; otherwise push each unvisited open neighbour with distance + 1, marking it visited when pushed.

Marking on push (not on pop) guarantees each cell enters the queue once, and BFS order guarantees the first arrival at any cell is along a shortest route. Total work is O(n²) with 8 neighbour checks per cell. If the queue empties without reaching the target, no clear path exists.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
desc:
prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You may complete as many buy/sell transactions as you like, subject to these rules:

  • you can hold at most one share at a time, so you must sell before buying again;
  • after you sell, you cannot buy on the very next day (one day of cooldown);
  • a share bought on day i can be sold on any later day.

Return the maximum total profit you can make. If no profitable trade exists, the answer is 0.
hints: At the end of any day you are in one of a few situations: holding a share, not holding and free to buy, or just sold and in cooldown.
Track the best profit for each of the three states and update them day by day: hold = max(hold, free - price), sold = hold_prev + price, free = max(free, sold_prev).
Be careful to use the previous day's values on the right-hand side, so compute new values in a temporary step. The answer is the larger of the 'free' and 'sold' states on the last day.
editorial: Define three values at the end of day i: hold is the best profit while owning a share, sold is the best profit if you sold today (so tomorrow is a cooldown), and free is the best profit while owning nothing and being allowed to buy tomorrow.

Transitions for price p: hold' = max(hold, free - p) (keep, or buy today from the free state); sold' = hold + p (sell today); free' = max(free, sold) (rest, or finish yesterday's cooldown). Start with hold = -infinity, sold = 0, free = 0. After the last day the answer is max(sold, free); ending while still holding a share can never be better. Only O(1) values are kept, so the space is constant.

title: Longest Balanced Binary Subarray
desc:
You are given a binary array bits containing only 0 and 1. A contiguous subarray is balanced if it contains the same number of zeros and ones.

Return the length of the longest balanced subarray, or 0 if there is none.

For example, [0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0] gives 4.
hints: Checking every subarray works in O(n<sup>2</sup>). What running quantity decides whether a subarray is balanced?
Treat each 0 as -1 and each 1 as +1. A balanced subarray is exactly one whose sum is 0.
A subarray sums to 0 when two prefix sums are equal. Store the earliest index at which each prefix sum occurred, and measure the distance to later repeats.
editorial: Map 0 to -1 and 1 to +1 and keep a running prefix sum s. The subarray between positions i (exclusive) and j (inclusive) is balanced exactly when prefix[i] == prefix[j].

Keep a hash map from each prefix value to the first index where it appeared, seeded with {0: -1} for the empty prefix. At each index j, if the current prefix was seen before at i, the length j - i is a candidate; otherwise record j. Never overwrite an earlier index, since the earliest one gives the longest subarray. One pass, O(n) time.

title: Count Subarrays with Sum Divisible by K
desc:
Given an integer array nums (values may be negative) and a positive integer k, count the non-empty contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by k.

Subarrays at different positions count separately even if they hold the same values. A sum of 0 is divisible by every k.

For example, nums = [4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1] and k = 5 give 7.
hints: Write a subarray sum as the difference of two prefix sums. When is that difference divisible by k?
Two prefix sums give a divisible difference exactly when they leave the same remainder modulo k.
Count how many earlier prefixes (including the empty one) share each remainder. Normalise negative remainders into 0..k-1 before counting.
editorial: Let P[i] be the sum of the first i elements, with P[0] = 0. The subarray covering elements i..j-1 has sum P[j] - P[i], which is divisible by k iff P[j] % k == P[i] % k.

Walk through the array keeping a counter of remainders of the prefixes seen so far, starting with remainder 0 counted once for the empty prefix. For each new prefix remainder m, add the current count of m to the answer, then increment it. In languages where % can return a negative value, use ((x % k) + k) % k. With n prefixes that is O(n) time.

title: Longest Subarray with Sum K
desc:
Given an integer array nums that may contain negative numbers, zeros and positives, and an integer k, return the length of the longest contiguous subarray whose elements add up to exactly k.

If no subarray has that sum, return 0.

For example, nums = [1, -1, 5, -2, 3] and k = 3 give 4, from the subarray [1, -1, 5, -2].
hints: A sliding window needs non-negative numbers to know when to shrink. With mixed signs it fails, so think about prefix sums.
A subarray sums to k when prefix[j] - prefix[i] = k. For the current prefix, which earlier prefix value are you looking for?
Store, for each prefix sum, only its first index. At each position look up prefix - k and measure the distance.
editorial: Let prefix be the running sum after the current element. A subarray that ends here and sums to k must start right after a position whose prefix sum was prefix - k. To make the subarray as long as possible we want the earliest such position.

Keep a map from prefix sum to the first index at which it occurred, seeded with {0: -1}. For each index j, if prefix - k is in the map at index i, the candidate length is j - i. Insert the current prefix only if it is not already present, so earlier indices are never overwritten. This runs in O(n) time; a two-pointer window is not valid because negative values break monotonicity.

title: Four Array Sum Zero Count
desc:
You are given four integer arrays a, b, c and d, all of the same length n. Count the index tuples (i, j, k, l), each index in 0..n-1, such that

a[i] + b[j] + c[k] + d[l] == 0.

Tuples that differ in any index are counted separately, even if the values are equal.

For example, a = [1, 2], b = [-2, -1], c = [-1, 2], d = [0, 2] give 2.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200 (all four arrays have length n)
hints: Four nested loops cost O(n<sup>4</sup>). That is far too slow for n = 200.
Split the four arrays into two pairs. Every sum a[i] + b[j] must be cancelled by some c[k] + d[l].
Count all pair sums of a and b in a hash map. Then, for each pair sum of c and d, add the count stored for its negation.
editorial: Meet in the middle. Enumerate all n2 sums a[i] + b[j] and store how many times each sum occurs in a hash map. Then enumerate all n2 sums c[k] + d[l]; each one pairs with exactly map[-(c[k] + d[l])] tuples from the first half.

This takes O(n<sup>2</sup>) time and space instead of O(n<sup>4</sup>). Because the answer counts tuples, not distinct value combinations, the map must store multiplicities rather than just presence. For n = 200 the answer is at most 200<sup>4</sup> = 1.6 billion, which still fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

title: Max Pair Sum with Equal Digit Sum
desc:
The digit sum of a positive integer is the sum of its decimal digits, so the digit sum of 4807 is 19.

From the array nums of positive integers, choose two elements at different indices whose digit sums are equal, so that their total value is as large as possible. Return that maximum total, or -1 if no two elements share a digit sum.

For example, [18, 43, 36, 13, 7] gives 54, from 18 + 36 (both have digit sum 9).
hints: Comparing every pair is O(n<sup>2</sup>). Group numbers by something cheaper to compare.
Numbers can only be paired if they have the same digit sum, so use the digit sum as a grouping key.
Within one group only the two largest values matter. Track the best value seen per digit sum and combine it with each new number from that group.
editorial: Compute the digit sum of each number. For each digit sum keep the largest value seen so far in a hash map. When a new number x with digit sum s arrives and the map already holds a best value m for s, then x + m is the best pair ending at x; update the global answer, then store max(m, x).

Since a pair needs two elements, the answer is only defined when some group has at least two numbers; otherwise return -1. Digit sums here are at most 81, so even a plain array of size 82 works as the map. Overall O(n log M) for digit extraction. The largest possible total is 2 * 10<sup>9</sup>, which fits in a signed 32-bit integer.

title: Next Permutation
desc:
Consider all distinct orderings of the numbers in nums, listed in increasing lexicographic order (compare the first elements, then the second, and so on). Return the ordering that comes right after nums in that list.

If nums is already the last (largest) ordering, return the first (smallest) one, which is the elements in non-decreasing order. The array may contain duplicates, and a solution needs only O(1) extra space besides the result.

[1, 2, 3] -> [1, 3, 2]
[3, 2, 1] -> [1, 2, 3]
[1, 1, 5] -> [1, 5, 1]
hints: Look at the array from the right. The longest non-increasing suffix is already the largest possible arrangement of its elements, so nothing inside it can be made bigger.
Find the rightmost index i with nums[i] < nums[i + 1]. Element i must grow, and everything to its right should then be as small as possible.
Swap nums[i] with the rightmost element greater than it (it lies in the suffix), then reverse the suffix after position i so it becomes ascending. If no such i exists, just reverse the whole array.
editorial: Scan from the right for the first position i where nums[i] < nums[i + 1]. Everything after i is non-increasing, which is the biggest arrangement of those values, so to get the next permutation the prefix up to i must change and nums[i] must be replaced by the smallest larger value available in the suffix.

That value is the rightmost suffix element strictly greater than nums[i] (rightmost because the suffix is non-increasing, so it is the smallest of the larger ones, and picking the rightmost keeps duplicates consistent). Swap the two. The suffix is still non-increasing, so reversing it gives the smallest arrangement of the suffix, which is exactly what the next permutation needs.
If no i exists, the whole array is non-increasing, the last permutation, and reversing it wraps around to the first. Time is O(n) with a constant number of passes.
solution:
def nextPermutation(nums):
    a = list(nums)
    n = len(a)
    i = n - 2
    while i >= 0 and a[i] >= a[i + 1]:
        i -= 1
    if i >= 0:
        j = n - 1
        while a[j] <= a[i]:
            j -= 1
        a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    lo, hi = i + 1, n - 1
    while lo < hi:
        a[lo], a[hi] = a[hi], a[lo]
        lo += 1
        hi -= 1
    return a

title: Sort Colors (Dutch Flag)
desc:
Every element of nums is 0, 1 or 2 (think of red, white and blue pieces of cloth). Rearrange the array so that all the 0s come first, then all the 1s, then all the 2s, and return the rearranged array.

Use a library sort only as a last resort: the point of this exercise is a single pass over the array with O(1) extra space, without counting the values first.

nums = [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]
result = [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]
hints: Counting how many of each value there are and rewriting the array works in two passes. Can you do it in one?
Maintain three regions: a block of 0s at the front, a block of 2s at the back, and an unexamined middle. A 1 can simply stay where it is.
Use pointers lo, i, hi. If nums[i] is 0, swap it to lo and advance both; if it is 2, swap it to hi and move only hi down (the swapped-in value is still unknown); if it is 1, just advance i.
editorial: This is the Dutch national flag partition. Keep the invariant that nums[0:lo] are all 0, nums[lo:i] are all 1, nums[hi+1:] are all 2, and nums[i:hi+1] are not yet classified.

Look at nums[i]. A 0 is swapped with nums[lo] (which is a 1 or is the same cell) and both lo and i move forward. A 2 is swapped with nums[hi] and hi moves back, but i stays put because the element that arrived from the right has not been inspected yet. A 1 is already in the correct region, so i advances. The loop ends when i passes hi.
Every step shrinks the unclassified region by one cell, so the time is O(n) in a single pass with O(1) extra space.

title: Flight Bookings Seat Totals
desc:
An airline operates n flights numbered 1 to n. Each booking is a triple [first, last, seats], meaning seats seats were reserved on every flight from number first to number last inclusive.

Return an array of length n whose element at index i is the total number of seats reserved on flight i + 1.

n = 5, bookings = [[1, 2, 10], [2, 3, 20], [2, 5, 25]]
result = [10, 55, 45, 25, 25]
hints: Adding seats to every flight of a booking costs O(n) per booking. With 10,000 bookings that is too slow in the worst case.
Record only the changes: at flight first the running total goes up by seats, and just after last it goes back down by seats.
Store diff[first] += seats and diff[last + 1] -= seats (size n + 2), then take the running sum of diff to recover every flight's total.
editorial: This is the difference array technique. Instead of updating a whole range, mark where the contribution of a booking starts and where it stops: add seats at index first and subtract seats at index last + 1.

A single left-to-right running sum over the difference array then gives, at each flight, the sum of all bookings that are currently active. Processing the bookings costs O(1) each and the final sweep costs O(n), for O(n + m) time overall and O(n) space.
The totals never exceed 10,000 bookings times 10,000 seats, that is 10<sup>8</sup>, so 32-bit integers suffice.
solution:
def flightBookings(n, bookings):
    diff = [0] * (n + 2)
    for first, last, seats in bookings:
        diff[first] += seats
        diff[last + 1] -= seats
    out = []
    run = 0
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        run += diff[i]
        out.append(run)
    return out

title: Car Pooling Capacity Check
desc:
A minibus drives along a straight road in one direction and never turns back. It holds at most capacity passengers at any moment. Each trip is a triple [passengers, from, to]: a group of that many people gets on at position from and gets off at position to.

When a group leaves at position x and another group boards at the same position x, the leaving group is already gone before the new one boards. Return true if the bus can serve every trip without ever exceeding its capacity, otherwise false.

trips = [[2, 1, 5], [3, 3, 7]], capacity = 4  -> false  (positions 3 to 5 carry 5 people)
trips = [[2, 1, 5], [3, 5, 7]], capacity = 3  -> true
hints: The load on the bus only changes at the positions where somebody boards or leaves, so checking just those positions is enough.
Turn every trip into two events: +passengers at from and -passengers at to. Order the events by position.

At equal positions process the drop-offs before the boardings (sorting (position, delta) pairs does exactly this). Keep a running load and fail the moment it exceeds the capacity. Alternatively, use a difference array over positions 0..100,000.
editorial: Model the bus load as a function of position. A trip raises the load by passengers on the half-open stretch [from, to), so the load is the sum of all active trips. The question becomes whether the maximum of that function exceeds the capacity.

Create the events (from, +passengers) and (to, -passengers), sort them (negative deltas sort before positive ones at the same position, which implements the rule that leaving passengers are off before new ones board), and sweep while keeping a running total. If the total ever exceeds capacity, the answer is false.

Since positions are bounded by 100,000, a difference array over the positions gives the same result without sorting: add at from, subtract at to, then prefix-sum and compare each value with the capacity. Sorting costs O(m log m); the array approach costs O(m + P) where P is the largest position.

title: Intersection of Two Interval Lists
desc:
You are given two lists of closed intervals [start, end]. Inside each list the intervals are sorted by start and pairwise disjoint (no two of them share a point). The two lists may overlap each other freely.

Return the intersection of the two lists as a list of closed intervals, sorted by start. Two intervals that touch at a single point intersect in that point, for example [1, 3] and [3, 5] intersect in [3, 3].

firstList  = [[0, 2], [5, 10], [13, 23], [24, 25]]
secondList = [[1, 5], [8, 12], [15, 24], [25, 26]]
result = [[1, 2], [5, 5], [8, 10], [15, 23], [24, 24], [25, 25]]
constraints: Within each list, start<sub>i+1</sub> > end<sub>i</sub> (sorted and disjoint)
hints: Take the first interval from each list. If they overlap, the overlap is [max(starts), min(ends)]; otherwise there is nothing to report for this pair.
After handling a pair, one of the two intervals can never intersect anything later. Which one?
Advance the pointer of the list whose current interval ends first (on ties, advancing either is fine). Because each list is sorted and disjoint, this visits every possible intersection in order.
editorial: Use two pointers i and j. For the current pair compute lo = max(a.start, b.start) and hi = min(a.end, b.end). If lo ≤ hi the pair intersects in [lo, hi], so append it (note that lo == hi is a valid single-point intersection).

Then discard the interval that finishes first: its right end is smaller, so every later interval in the other list starts beyond it and cannot overlap it, and the later intervals of its own list are disjoint from it. When the ends are equal both intervals are finished, and advancing one of them is enough because the other will then fail the overlap test and be advanced next.

Each step advances a pointer, so the total time is O(n + m) and the output is already sorted, since intersections are produced in increasing order of position. Comparing every pair would also be correct but costs O(n * m).

title: Boats to Carry People
desc:
A group of people needs to cross a river. weights[i] is the weight of person i. Every boat can carry at most two people at once, and the combined weight on a boat must not exceed limit.

Every person weighs at most limit, so everyone can always travel, even alone. Return the smallest number of boats needed to carry everybody.

weights = [3, 2, 2, 1], limit = 3
boats: [1, 2], [2], [3]
result = 3
hints: Each boat holds at most two people, so the answer is at least half the number of people. What decides how many pairs you can form?
Think about the heaviest remaining person. Who is the best partner for them, if any partner is possible at all?
Sort the weights. If the heaviest person can share a boat with the lightest remaining person, do it; otherwise the heaviest travels alone. Use two pointers.
editorial: Sort the weights. Consider the heaviest unassigned person. If even the lightest unassigned person cannot ride with them, nobody can, so they take a boat alone. Otherwise pairing them with the lightest person is never worse than pairing them with anyone else: the lightest is the most flexible partner, and using it here does not hurt anyone else's chances.

Implement this with a left pointer at the lightest and a right pointer at the heaviest. Each iteration uses one boat, always moves the right pointer in, and moves the left pointer in as well when the pair fits. The sort dominates, so the time is O(n log n) with O(n) space for the sorted copy.

title: Subarrays With Product Below K
desc:
You are given an array nums of positive integers and an integer k. Count the contiguous, non-empty subarrays whose elements multiply to a value strictly less than k.

Subarrays at different positions are counted separately even if their contents are identical.

nums = [10, 5, 2, 6], k = 100
result = 8
[10] [5] [2] [6] [10,5] [5,2] [2,6] [5,2,6]
hints: Checking every subarray is O(n²). Notice that every number is at least 1, so extending a subarray never decreases its product.
That monotonic behaviour means that if a window is too big, every longer window with the same start is too big as well.
Use a window [left, right] with a running product. After adding nums[right], shrink from the left while the product is at least k, then add right - left + 1 to the answer.
editorial: Fix the right end right. Because all values are positive integers, the product of nums[left..right] only grows as left moves to the left. So the valid starting points form one contiguous range ending at right, and the number of valid subarrays ending at right is exactly the window length.

Maintain the product incrementally: multiply by the new element, then divide by nums[left] while the product is too large (stop shrinking when left passes right, which handles k ≤ 1 where nothing qualifies). Each index enters and leaves the window once, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.

title: Longest Run of Ones After Deleting One
desc:
The array nums contains only 0 and 1. You must delete exactly one element (it may be a 0 or a 1). After the deletion the remaining elements close up with no gap.

Return the length of the longest block of consecutive 1s you can end up with. If the array has no 1 after the deletion, the answer is 0.

nums = [1, 1, 0, 1]
delete the 0 -> [1, 1, 1]
result = 3
hints: Deleting a 0 joins the run of ones on its left with the run on its right. Deleting a 1 only shortens a run.
Think of it as finding the longest window that contains at most one 0. The deleted element is that 0.

Slide a window, shrinking from the left whenever it holds two zeros. The answer is the largest window length minus 1, because one element must always be deleted, which also covers an array of all ones.
editorial: A window with at most one zero becomes a run of ones once that zero is deleted, and its length drops by one. If the window has no zero at all, we still have to delete one element, which again costs one. So the answer is max window length - 1 over all windows containing at most one zero.

Maintain the window [left, right] and a count of zeros inside it. When the count exceeds one, move left forward until it is back to one. A single pass gives O(n) time and O(1) space. Edge cases fall out naturally: an array of all zeros has windows of length 1, giving 0, and a single element gives 0.

title: Minimum Removals From the Ends to Reach a Sum
desc:
In one move you may delete either the first or the last element of nums, and you subtract the deleted value from x. Return the smallest number of moves that makes x exactly 0, or -1 if that cannot be done.

The array changes after every move, so later moves operate on what remains.

nums = [1, 1, 4, 2, 3], x = 5
remove 3 (right), then 2 (right): 5 - 3 - 2 = 0
result = 2
hints: Whatever you remove is some prefix plus some suffix of the array. What is left over?
The remaining middle part is a contiguous subarray whose sum equals sum(nums) - x. Fewest removals means longest middle.
All values are positive, so a variable-size sliding window can find the longest subarray with a given sum. Return n - longest, or -1 if no such subarray exists.
editorial: Removing elements from both ends leaves a contiguous block in the middle. If the removed values sum to x, the block sums to target = total - x. Minimising the moves is the same as maximising the block length.

If target < 0 the answer is -1. If target == 0 everything must be removed, so the answer is n. Otherwise, because all numbers are positive, a window sum grows when extended right and shrinks when the left edge moves, so a two-pointer sweep finds the longest subarray summing to target in O(n). The result is n - longest, or -1 if none was found.

title: 4Sum
desc:
Given an integer array nums and an integer target, return every distinct quadruplet of values [a, b, c, d] that can be chosen from four different positions of nums and satisfies a + b + c + d = target.

Two quadruplets are the same if they contain the same values, regardless of positions. Write each quadruplet in non-decreasing order; the order of the quadruplets in the result does not matter. Return an empty list when there is none.

nums = [1, 0, -1, 0, -2, 2], target = 0
result = [[-2,-1,1,2], [-2,0,0,2], [-1,0,0,1]]
hints: Four nested loops are O(n⁴). Can you reduce the problem step by step, as in 3Sum and Two Sum?
Sort the array. Fix the first two values with two loops, then find the other two with two pointers moving inward.
Skip repeated values at each of the four levels (first, second, and inside the pointer loop after a match) so each quadruplet is reported once.
editorial: Sort the array. Loop over the first value i, then over the second value j > i, and finish with lo = j + 1 and hi = n - 1. If the four-value sum is below the target, move lo right; if above, move hi left; if equal, record it and move both pointers past their duplicates.

To avoid duplicate quadruplets, skip a value at the i level when it equals the previous i value, likewise at the j level (only when j > i + 1), and skip equal neighbours after each match. Time is O(n³) after the O(n log n) sort, and extra space is O(1) besides the output.

title: Search a Flattened Sorted Grid
desc:
The m x n matrix grid has two properties: every row is sorted in strictly increasing order, and the first number of each row is larger than the last number of the previous row.

Return true if target appears anywhere in grid, otherwise false. Your solution should run in O(log(m * n)) time.
constraints: Reading the rows one after another yields a strictly increasing sequence
hints: A scan of all cells works but ignores the ordering. What does the ordering say about the whole grid?
If you wrote the rows one after another into a single list, that list would be sorted. You do not need to build it.
Binary search over indices 0 .. m*n - 1. Index i corresponds to the cell in row i // n and column i % n.
editorial: Because each row begins above where the previous one ended, the grid read in row-major order is one long strictly increasing array of m * n numbers. That is a standard sorted-array membership question.

Run a binary search on the virtual index range [0, m*n). For a middle index mid read grid[mid // n][mid % n] and compare it with the target, discarding the half that cannot contain it. This needs O(log(m * n)) time and O(1) space. A two-stage search (first find the row, then search inside it) has the same complexity.

title: Search a Rotated Array with Duplicates
desc:
A non-decreasing array (it may contain repeated values) was rotated to the left by an unknown number of positions. For example, [0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 5, 6] rotated by 4 becomes [2, 5, 6, 0, 0, 1, 2]. The rotation amount can also be 0.

Given the rotated array nums and an integer target, return true if target occurs in nums, otherwise false. Make the search as fast as you can; with duplicates the worst case cannot be better than linear, but typical inputs should take O(log n).
constraints: nums is a non-decreasing array rotated by some amount
hints: Without duplicates you could always tell which half of the middle is sorted. Where exactly do duplicates break that?
If nums[lo] < nums[mid] the left half is sorted; if nums[lo] > nums[mid] the right half is. Only equality leaves things ambiguous.

When nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] you cannot tell which side is sorted. Drop one element from each end (the middle already failed to match) and continue; otherwise decide which half is sorted, test if the target lies inside it, and narrow the range.
editorial: After a rotation, at least one of the two halves around mid is always sorted. Compare nums[lo] with nums[mid] to find it: if the left half is sorted and nums[lo] ≤ target < nums[mid], keep the left half; otherwise keep the right. The mirror reasoning applies when the right half is sorted.

Duplicates create one ambiguous case: nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi], for instance [1, 1, 1, 3, 1] versus [1, 3, 1, 1, 1]. Here neither half can be ruled out, so shrink the range by one from both ends (the values being equal to nums[mid], which was not the target, makes this safe). That step is what makes the worst case O(n), e.g. an array of all ones with a single different value, but typical inputs still run in O(log n). Space is O(1).

title: Lone Value in Sorted Pairs
desc:
The array nums is sorted in non-decreasing order. Every value in it appears exactly twice, except for one value that appears exactly once. Because equal values are adjacent, the equal pairs sit side by side.

Return the value that appears only once. Your solution must run in O(log n) time and use O(1) extra space.
constraints: nums is sorted; exactly one value appears once and every other value appears twice
hints: XOR-ing every element finds the answer in O(n). How could you throw away half of the array in O(1) instead?
Look at the pairs to the left of the lone value: the first copy sits at an even index and the second at an odd index. After the lone value, that alignment flips.

For a middle index, move it to the even index of its position (if it is odd, subtract one). If nums[mid] == nums[mid + 1] the left side is still aligned, so the lone value is to the right; otherwise it is at mid or to the left.
editorial: Before the lone element every pair starts on an even index, i.e. nums[2i] == nums[2i + 1]. After the lone element every pair starts on an odd index. The array length is odd, so the lone value always sits at an even index.

Binary search over even indices. Take mid and, if it is odd, decrease it by one so it points at the supposed first copy of a pair. If nums[mid] == nums[mid + 1] the pairs are still aligned up to mid + 1, so the answer lies at mid + 2 or later; set lo = mid + 2. Otherwise the alignment broke at or before mid, so set hi = mid. When lo == hi the lone value is found. Time O(log n), space O(1).

title: Earliest Day for Bouquets
desc:
A garden has a row of flowers; flower i blooms on day bloomDay[i] and stays bloomed afterwards. A bouquet needs k adjacent bloomed flowers, and each flower can be used in at most one bouquet.

Return the smallest day number by which you can have made m bouquets. If it is impossible, return -1.
hints: First rule out the impossible case: you need at least m * k flowers in total.
Fix a day d. Which flowers are bloomed? How many bouquets can you greedily make from runs of bloomed flowers?

If you can make m bouquets on day d, you can on every later day too. Binary search the day between the smallest and largest bloom day, counting bouquets with one left-to-right scan: extend a run for each bloomed flower, cash it in as one bouquet every time it reaches length k, and reset it on an unbloomed flower.
editorial: If m * k exceeds the number of flowers the answer is -1. Otherwise all flowers have bloomed on day max(bloomDay), so an answer exists.

For a fixed day d, scan the row: a bloomed flower extends the current run, and each time the run reaches k one bouquet is made and the run restarts; an unbloomed flower resets the run. This greedy count is the maximum number of bouquets for that day. The count never decreases as d increases, so binary search the smallest day with count ≥ m. With about 30 iterations of an O(n) scan the total is O(n log(max bloom day)) time and O(1) space.

title: Maximize the Minimum Gap Between Balls
desc:
There are baskets at the distinct integer coordinates in positions (in no particular order), each of which holds at most one ball. You must place exactly m balls into different baskets.

The gap of a placement is the smallest distance between any two of the chosen baskets. Return the largest gap that any placement can achieve.
hints: Trying every set of m baskets is hopeless for large inputs. Start by sorting the positions.
Turn the question around: given a required gap d, can you fit m balls so that neighbours are at least d apart? A greedy left-to-right placement answers that.
If gap d is achievable, so is any smaller gap. Binary search d from 1 to (max - min) // (m - 1), using the greedy check (take the leftmost basket, then the next basket at least d away, and so on).
editorial: Sort the positions. For a target gap d, place the first ball at the leftmost basket and keep placing each next ball in the nearest basket that is at least d beyond the previously placed one. This greedy choice leaves the most room for later balls, so it places the maximum number of balls for that d; the gap is feasible exactly when this number is at least m.

Feasibility is monotone in d, so binary search for the largest feasible value. The gap can never exceed (max - min) // (m - 1) and is at least 1 because positions are distinct. The cost is O(n log n) for sorting plus O(n log(max - min)) for the search.
time: O(n log n + n log R)

title: Kth Smallest in a Row- and Column-Sorted Grid
desc:
In the m x n matrix grid, every row is sorted in non-decreasing order from left to right, and every column is sorted in non-decreasing order from top to bottom. Values may repeat.

Return the k-th smallest value when all m * n cells are put in sorted order (so duplicates count separately: in [1, 1, 2] the 2nd smallest is 1). Try to avoid sorting all the cells.
constraints: Each row and each column is in non-decreasing order
hints: Flattening and sorting works in O(mn log(mn)). The row and column order should let you do better.
Instead of searching positions, search values: for a number x, how many cells are ≤ x? Can you count that without looking at every cell?

Count cells ≤ x by walking a staircase from the bottom-left corner: move up when the cell is greater than x, otherwise count the column prefix and move right. Binary search the smallest x in [grid[0][0], grid[m-1][n-1]] whose count is at least k.
editorial: The answer is a value that exists in the grid, lying between the top-left and bottom-right cells. Define count(x) as the number of cells with value ≤ x; it never decreases as x grows. The k-th smallest value is the smallest x with count(x) ≥ k, and that x is always an actual cell value, because count only jumps at values present in the grid.

Compute count(x) in O(m + n): begin at the bottom-left cell; if it exceeds x move up, otherwise all cells above it in this column are ≤ x, so add row + 1 and move right. Binary search over the value range takes about 31 iterations, for O((m + n) log(range)) time and O(1) space. A min-heap that pops k times is another option at O(k log m).

title: Next Greater Value in a Circular Array
desc:
The array nums is circular: the element after the last one is the first one again. For each position i, look at the elements that follow it, wrapping around the end of the array, and find the first one that is strictly larger than nums[i]. You may look at the other n - 1 positions at most once each; position i itself is never a candidate.

Return an array answer where answer[i] is that larger value, or -1 if no element of the array is strictly larger than nums[i].
hints: Brute force scans up to n positions for each element, which is O(n<sup>2</sup>). To handle the wrap-around, imagine the array written twice in a row.
Process the doubled array from left to right and keep a stack of positions whose answer is still unknown. A new value resolves every waiting position with a smaller value.
Only push positions during the first pass (index < n). The second pass exists solely to resolve the elements that are waiting for a greater value on the wrapped-around side.
editorial: Use a monotonic stack of indices whose values are non-increasing from bottom to top. Walk k from 0 to 2n - 1 and let i = k mod n. While the stack is non-empty and nums[stack.top] < nums[i], pop it and set its answer to nums[i]. During the first lap (k < n) push i afterwards.

Because the second lap only resolves waiting indices and never pushes, each index is pushed and popped at most once, giving O(n) time. Indices that are still on the stack after both laps hold the global maximum value (or ties with it), so they keep the answer -1. The array is initialised with -1 for exactly that reason.

title: Sum of Subarray Minimums
desc:
For every contiguous, non-empty subarray of arr, take its smallest element. Return the sum of all these minimums.

The sum can be huge, so return it modulo 1,000,000,007.
hints: There are O(n<sup>2</sup>) subarrays. Instead of enumerating them, ask for each element: in how many subarrays is it the minimum?

Element arr[i] is the minimum of a subarray exactly when the subarray lies strictly between the nearest smaller element on its left and the nearest smaller element on its right. Ties must be broken consistently so a subarray is counted once.
Find, with a monotonic stack, the distance left to the previous strictly smaller element and right to the next smaller-or-equal element. Then arr[i] contributes arr[i] * left * right.
editorial: Count contributions. Let L be the number of choices for the left end of a subarray in which arr[i] is the chosen minimum (distance back to the previous element that is strictly smaller) and R the number of choices for the right end (distance forward to the next element that is smaller or equal). Any left end and right end combine, so arr[i] is the minimum of exactly L * R subarrays. Using strict on one side and non-strict on the other makes sure that among equal values only one is credited for each subarray.

Both distances come from monotonic stacks in a single pass each, so the whole computation is O(n). Sum arr[i] * L * R over all i, taking the remainder modulo 1,000,000,007 as you go (Python integers do not overflow, but fixed-width languages need the modulus applied to avoid overflow).
solution:
def sumSubarrayMins(arr):
    MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7
    n = len(arr)
    left = [0] * n    # choices of left end: distance to previous strictly smaller element
    right = [0] * n   # choices of right end: distance to next smaller-or-equal element
    stack = []
    for i in range(n):
        while stack and arr[stack[-1]] >= arr[i]:
            stack.pop()
        left[i] = i - (stack[-1] if stack else -1)
        stack.append(i)
    stack = []
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        while stack and arr[stack[-1]] > arr[i]:
            stack.pop()
        right[i] = (stack[-1] if stack else n) - i
        stack.append(i)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        total = (total + arr[i] * left[i] * right[i]) % MOD
    return total

title: Remove K Digits for the Smallest Number
desc:
The string num is a non-negative integer written in decimal. Delete exactly k of its digits (the remaining digits keep their original order) so that the number they form is as small as possible.

Return the result as a string without leading zeros. If every digit is deleted, or the remaining digits form the value zero, return "0".
constraints: num contains only digits and has no leading zeros (except the single digit "0")
hints: Compare two numbers with the same number of digits: the leftmost differing digit decides. So you want small digits as far to the left as possible.
When a digit is followed by a smaller digit, deleting the first one makes the number smaller. Deleting from the left is always at least as good as deleting from the right.

Use a stack of kept digits. For each new digit, while you still have deletions left and the top of the stack is larger than the new digit, pop. Afterwards drop any remaining deletions from the end and strip leading zeros.
editorial: Greedy with a monotonic stack. Keep the digits chosen so far on a stack. When a new digit d arrives and the top of the stack is larger than d, removing that top digit makes the number strictly smaller (a smaller digit moves into a more significant position), so pop while k > 0 and the top is larger, then push d.

If digits remain to delete after the scan, the stack is non-decreasing, so the best choice is to delete from the end. Finally, strip leading zeros and return "0" if nothing is left. Each digit is pushed and popped at most once, so the time is O(n).

title: Asteroid Collision Survivors
desc:
Asteroids travel along a line, listed from left to right in the array asteroids. The absolute value of an entry is the asteroid's size, and its sign is its direction: positive moves to the right, negative moves to the left. All asteroids move at the same speed.

Two asteroids collide only when a right-moving one is somewhere to the left of a left-moving one and nothing separates them. In a collision the smaller asteroid is destroyed; if both have the same size, both are destroyed. Asteroids that move in the same direction never meet, and an asteroid that has no one to collide with keeps flying.

Return the asteroids that survive after all collisions are over, in their original left-to-right order.
hints: Only a right-moving asteroid followed (somewhere later) by a left-moving one can ever collide. Think about what a left-moving asteroid meets first.
Process asteroids from left to right. The right-movers seen so far that are still alive form a stack; the closest one is on top.

A new left-mover keeps fighting the top of the stack while that top is a right-mover: pop it if it is smaller, pop both if equal, or stop if the new asteroid is destroyed. If the new asteroid survives, push it.
editorial: Keep a stack of surviving asteroids. A new right-moving asteroid can never collide with anything already processed (everything to its left either moves left and has escaped, or moves right at the same speed), so it is simply pushed. A new left-moving asteroid collides with the nearest right-mover on the stack, if there is one.

Loop: while the new asteroid is alive and the top of the stack is positive, compare sizes. If the top is smaller it explodes and we continue with the next stack element; if they are equal both explode and we stop; if the top is larger the new asteroid explodes. If it is still alive when the loop ends it is pushed (it only sits on top of left-movers or an empty stack). Every asteroid is pushed and popped at most once, so the time is O(n).

title: Valid Stack Push and Pop Order
desc:
Starting from an empty stack, you push the values of pushed onto it in exactly the given order. Between pushes you may pop the top of the stack as often as you like (while it is non-empty), and every popped value is recorded in the order of popping. You may stop pushing early, but all values must eventually be pushed and popped.

The values in pushed are distinct, and popped is a permutation of pushed. Return true if some interleaving of pushes and pops makes the recorded pop order equal to popped, and false otherwise.
constraints: -10<sup>9</sup> ≤ pushed[i] ≤ 10<sup>9</sup>, all values in pushed are distinct
popped is a permutation of pushed
hints: You never get to choose which element a pop returns, so the order in which values are popped is heavily constrained. Simulating is easier than reasoning abstractly.
Whenever the top of your stack equals the next value that must be popped, popping right away is never harmful.
Push values one by one; after each push pop as long as the top matches the next expected popped value. At the end the stack must be empty.
editorial: Simulate with a real stack and a pointer j into popped. Push each value of pushed; after each push, while the stack is non-empty and its top equals popped[j], pop it and advance j.

The greedy pop is safe: if the top equals the next required value, any alternative would push more elements above it, and then it could only be popped after those, which would break the required order. If the stack is empty after all pushes have been processed the sequence is valid, otherwise some value is trapped under others in the wrong order. Time O(n), space O(n).

title: Detect a 132 Pattern
desc:
A 132 pattern in an integer array is a choice of three positions i < j < k whose values satisfy nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j]: the middle value is the largest, the last value lies strictly between the other two, and the first is the smallest.

Return true if nums contains a 132 pattern, otherwise return false.
hints: Trying all triples is O(n<sup>3</sup>). Fix the middle (largest) value and think about what the best first and last values would be.
Scan from right to left, so that the '2' is seen first, then the '3', then the '1'. Remember the largest value seen so far that already has a larger value to its left.

Maintain a stack of candidates for '3' and a variable third for the best '2'. When the current value is smaller than third, you have found '1'. Otherwise pop every stack value smaller than the current value into third and push the current value.
editorial: Traverse the array from right to left. We look for the pattern in reverse: first a '2' (value third), then a larger '3' that appears before it in the array, and finally a '1' even earlier that is smaller than the '2'. Keep a stack of values that are '3' candidates, and let third be the largest value ever popped from the stack: each popped value was smaller than some value that came before it in the array, so it is a valid '2' with a larger '3' on its left.

For the current value x: if x < third there is a 132 pattern with x as the '1', so return true. Otherwise, while the stack top is smaller than x, pop it and raise third to it (the larger x is the '3' for these), then push x. Maximising third is optimal because it makes the check x < third easiest to satisfy. Each element is pushed and popped once: O(n) time, O(n) space.

title: Integer to Roman Numeral
desc:
Convert a positive integer to its Roman numeral, written with lowercase symbols: i=1, v=5, x=10, l=50, c=100, d=500, m=1000.

The numeral is built from the decimal digits of the number, thousands first. Each non-zero digit is written with its own symbols and zero digits are skipped. Inside one digit the symbols are written largest to smallest and added, except for the six subtractive forms iv=4, ix=9, xl=40, xc=90, cd=400, cm=900. A symbol is never repeated more than three times in a row.

For example, 3 becomes "iii", 58 becomes "lviii" and 1994 becomes "mcmxciv".
hints: Think of the number one decimal digit at a time. The digit 7 in the tens place is worth 70, which is written lxx.

Each digit position has its own trio of symbols (one, five, ten), such as x, l, c for the tens place. The digit then decides the pattern: 1-3 repeat the 'one' symbol, 4 is one+five, 5-8 is five followed by up to three 'ones', 9 is one+ten.

Alternatively, list all thirteen values in descending order (1000, 900, 500, 400, 100, 90, 50, 40, 10, 9, 5, 4, 1) with their symbols and greedily take the largest value that still fits, appending its symbols each time.
editorial: The greedy method works because the table of thirteen values already contains the six subtractive forms as if they were single symbols. Go through the table from large to small and, while the remaining number is at least the current value, append its symbol string and subtract the value. Because the table is sorted and contains every allowed token, the first token that fits is always the correct next piece of the standard numeral.

The digit-by-digit method gives the same result: split the number into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones and look up each part in a small pattern table. Both approaches do a constant amount of work, since the output never exceeds 15 symbols.

title: Multiply Decimal Strings
desc:
The strings num1 and num2 each hold a non-negative integer in decimal. Return their product as a string.

The numbers can have hundreds of digits, so they do not fit in the built-in integer types. Do the multiplication yourself on the digits, the way it is done by hand, instead of converting the whole strings to integers.

For example, "12" × "12" is "144", and "123" × "0" is "0".
constraints: num1 and num2 contain only digits 0-9
Neither number has leading zeros, except the number 0 itself
hints: Remember long multiplication: every digit of one number multiplies every digit of the other, and the partial products are added at shifted positions.
The product of a digit at position i (counted from the right in num1) and one at position j in num2 contributes to position i + j of the result. The result has at most n + m digits.
Accumulate all products into an array of size n + m first, then do one pass from the lowest position upward to propagate carries. Finally strip leading zeros, keeping at least one digit.
editorial: Reverse both numbers so that index 0 is the ones digit. Allocate res of length n + m. For each pair (i, j), add a[i] * b[j] to res[i + j]. No entry can get large, since each holds at most min(n, m) products of at most 81 each.

Then make one carry pass: for k from 0 upward, total = res[k] + carry, store total % 10 and carry total // 10. Drop leading zeros from the high end (leave a single 0 if the product is zero) and reverse the digits into a string. The running time is O(n · m), which is fine for 200 digits.

title: Zigzag Conversion
desc:
Write the characters of s in a zigzag over numRows rows: go down one character per row from the first row to the last, then go diagonally up one character per row until you are back at the first row, and repeat. Then read the rows one after another, top to bottom, left to right, and join them into a new string.

For s = "paypalishiring" and numRows = 3 the layout is

p   a   h   n
a p l s i i g
y   i   r

and the answer is "pahnaplsiigyir". With numRows = 1 the string is returned unchanged.
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters and digits
hints: You do not need to build the 2D picture. The only thing that matters is which row each character lands on.

Walk through the string keeping a current row and a direction. The row goes 0, 1, ..., numRows-1, then back down numRows-2, ..., 0 and so on. Flip the direction at the first and last rows (careful when numRows == 1).

Append each character to the bucket of its row, then join the buckets. For an O(1)-extra-space version, use the cycle length 2 * (numRows - 1): row r takes the characters at r + k*cycle and cycle*(k+1) - r.
editorial: Simulation: keep a list of numRows buckets. For each character, append it to the bucket for the current row, then move the row by +1 or -1. When the row reaches 0 or numRows-1, reverse the direction. The special case numRows = 1 (or numRows ≥ len(s)) returns s directly, since there is no zigzag to speak of. Concatenating the buckets gives the answer in O(n).

Direct indexing works too. The pattern repeats every cycle = 2 * (numRows - 1) characters. In row r, the characters at indices r, r + cycle, r + 2*cycle, ... belong to the 'vertical' strokes, and for rows strictly between the first and the last there is one extra character per cycle, at index k*cycle + cycle - r, on the diagonal stroke.

title: Longest Substring With Every Character Repeated K Times
desc:
Given a string s and an integer k, find the longest substring of s in which every character that appears does so at least k times within that substring. Return its length, or 0 if no such substring exists.

For example, for s = "aaabb" and k = 3 the answer is 3 (the substring "aaa"), for s = "ababbc" and k = 2 it is 5 (the substring "ababb"), and for s = "abc" and k = 2 it is 0.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Checking every substring with a frequency table is O(n²) and too slow for 20,000 characters. Look for characters that can never be part of an answer.
Count the letters of the whole string. A letter that occurs fewer than k times in total cannot occur k times in any substring, so no valid substring contains it.

Split the string at every such letter and solve each piece on its own, using the same rule again. If a piece has no rare letter at all, it is valid as a whole. The recursion is at most 26 levels deep.
editorial: Divide and conquer. Count the characters of the current segment. If every character occurs at least k times, the whole segment is valid and its length is returned. Otherwise, any character with count below k can never belong to a valid substring inside this segment (its count in a sub-segment is at most its count here), so cut the segment at each occurrence of such characters and recurse on the pieces; the answer is the best piece.

Each recursion level removes at least one distinct letter from consideration, so the depth is at most 26 and each level scans every character at most once: O(26 · n) time. A sliding window variant also works: for each target number of distinct letters from 1 to 26, run a window that keeps exactly that many distinct letters and tracks how many of them have reached k.

title: Longest Substring With Even Vowel Counts
desc:
Given a string s of lowercase letters, find the longest substring in which each of the five vowels a, e, i, o, u appears an even number of times (zero counts as even). Return its length.

The empty substring always qualifies, so the answer is never negative. For example, in "bcbcbc" there are no vowels at all, so the answer is 6; in "aeiou" the best substring is empty, so the answer is 0; in "aabeb" the answer is 3 ("aab").
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Trying every substring and counting its vowels is O(n²). Think about prefixes instead of substrings.
Only the parity (odd or even) of each vowel count matters, so the state of a prefix fits in 5 bits.

A substring has all-even counts exactly when the prefix before it and the prefix at its end have the same parity mask. Store the first index at which each of the 32 masks appears, and at every position look up the current mask.
