If there is no such balloon on a side, use 1 for that side.

Return the maximum number of coins you can collect by bursting every balloon. With no balloons, the answer is 0.
hints: Choosing which balloon to burst first splits the row in a way that makes the two parts depend on each other. Try thinking about which balloon is burst last instead.
If balloon k is the last one to burst inside the open range (l, r), its neighbours at that moment are exactly l and r, and the two sides (l, k) and (k, r) are independent subproblems.

Pad the array with a 1 at both ends. Let dp[l][r] be the best total for the balloons strictly between l and r. Then dp[l][r] = max over k of dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + a[l]*a[k]*a[r]. Fill by increasing interval length.
editorial: Pad the array: a = [1] + nums + [1]. Define dp[l][r] as the maximum coins from bursting all balloons strictly between indices l and r. Pick k as the balloon that bursts last in that range: at that time only l and r are left beside it, so it yields a[l] * a[k] * a[r], and the balloons on each side were burst earlier within their own independent ranges. So dp[l][r] = max_k (dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + a[l]*a[k]*a[r]), filled by increasing gap r - l. The answer is dp[0][n+1].

Thinking about the first balloon to burst fails because after removing it, its neighbours become adjacent and the subproblems are no longer independent. Choosing the last one fixes this. There are O(n²) ranges and O(n) choices of k each, hence O(n³) in total; with n = 300 and values at most 100 the answer stays well below 2<sup>31</sup>.

title: Regular Expression Matching
desc:
Implement a tiny pattern matcher. Given a text s and a pattern p, return true if the pattern matches the entire text, and false otherwise.

The pattern supports two special characters. . matches any single character. * means "zero or more copies of the element right before it", where that element is either a letter or a .. For example a* matches "", a, aaa, and .* matches any string at all. The pattern is well-formed: a * never appears first and never directly follows another *.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
p contains only lowercase English letters, '.' and '*'
In p, every '*' has a letter or '.' directly before it
hints: Compare the pattern and the text from the front. A plain character or '.' consumes exactly one text character; the interesting case is a '*'.

Let match(i, j) say whether s[i:] matches p[j:]. If p[j+1] is '*', you either skip the pair p[j], p[j+1] entirely, or (when s[i] fits p[j]) consume one text character and stay on the same pattern position.
Fill a table from the ends toward the front, or memoise the recursion. There are only (|s|+1) x (|p|+1) distinct states.
editorial: Define dp[i][j] as true when s[i:] matches p[j:]. The base case is dp[|s|][|p|] = true. For a state, let first be true when i < |s| and p[j] is equal to s[i] or is '.'. If p[j+1] is '*', then dp[i][j] = dp[i][j+2] or (first and dp[i+1][j]): use zero copies, or use one copy and stay on the same starred element. Otherwise dp[i][j] = first and dp[i+1][j+1].

Filling the table from the bottom-right corner needs only two rows at a time. A plain recursion without memoisation repeats the same states exponentially often (patterns like a*a*a*a*b are the classic killer), which is why the table matters. Because the whole text must match, an empty text can still match a pattern like a*b*.

title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
desc:
Given an array nums of positive integers and an integer k, decide whether the numbers can be divided into exactly k non-empty groups so that every group has the same sum. Each element must go into exactly one group.

Return true if such a division exists and false otherwise.
hints: If the total is not divisible by k, or some number is larger than total / k, the answer is immediately false. Otherwise every group must sum to target = total / k.
Fill the groups one after another: pick unused numbers until the current group reaches target, then start the next group.

With at most 16 numbers, the set of used numbers fits in a bitmask. The current group's partial sum is determined by the mask (it is sum(mask) mod target), so you can remember masks from which no solution exists and never explore them again.
editorial: Let target = total / k. Search over bitmasks of used numbers: from a mask, add any unused number that keeps the current group at most target; when the group sum reaches target it resets to zero. If the mask with all bits set is reached, the answer is true. Because the partial group sum depends only on the mask, a mask that failed once can be stored in a set and skipped, so there are at most 2n states, each tried with n choices: O(n · 2n).

Plain backtracking that places each number into one of k buckets can take k<sup>n</sup> steps on unlucky inputs, which is why the memo matters. Sorting the numbers ascending allows an early break as soon as a number does not fit, and skipping a number equal to an unused predecessor avoids retrying identical choices. An equivalent bottom-up DP stores, for each mask, the partial sum of the current group, or -1 if the mask cannot be reached.

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
desc:
You are given an integer matrix. Starting from any cell, you may repeatedly step to a cell directly above, below, left or right, as long as the value in the new cell is strictly larger than the value in the current cell. You cannot leave the matrix.

Return the largest number of cells on any such path (a path of a single cell has length 1).
hints: Treat each cell as a node, with an arrow from a cell to every neighbour that holds a larger value. Because values strictly grow, this graph has no cycles.
Define best(cell) as the longest path that starts there. It equals 1 plus the maximum of best(neighbour) over larger neighbours.

Compute it in order of decreasing value, so every larger neighbour is already done. Equivalently, process cells by increasing value and let each cell extend the best path ending at a smaller neighbour.
editorial: Sort all cells by value. Walk through them from smallest to largest; for each cell, len[cell] = 1 + max(len[nb]) over neighbours with a strictly smaller value (those were processed earlier, and equal values never count). The answer is the maximum of len. Sorting makes the order explicit, so there is no recursion at all, which matters for a 100 × 100 snake-shaped matrix where a recursive DFS would go 10,000 levels deep.

A memoised DFS from every cell gives the same result and is shorter to write when recursion depth is not a concern. A third way is a topological sort: peel off cells with no smaller neighbour layer by layer, and the number of layers is the answer. Each approach does O(R · C) work per cell-visit; sorting adds the log factor.

title: Distinct Subsequences
desc:
Given two strings s and t, count in how many different ways t can be obtained as a subsequence of s. A subsequence keeps the original order of the characters it keeps; two ways are different if they use a different set of positions in s, even when the resulting letters are the same.

For example, t = "rabbit" can be picked from s = "rabbbit" in 3 ways (any one of the three bs can be left out), and t = "bag" can be picked from s = "babgbag" in 5 ways. If t cannot be formed, return 0.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase letters and digits
The answer (and every intermediate count in the standard table) fits in a signed 32-bit integer
hints: Enumerating every subsequence of s is exponential. Look at the last character of s and ask how it can be used.

Let ways[i][j] be the number of ways to form the first j characters of t from the first i characters of s. The last character of s is either skipped or, if it equals t[j-1], used as the last character of the match.
ways[i][j] = ways[i-1][j] + (ways[i-1][j-1] if s[i-1] == t[j-1] else 0), with ways[i][0] = 1. The table can be compressed to one row if j is iterated downwards.
editorial: Use dynamic programming over prefixes. Let ways[i][j] be the number of ways the prefix t[:j] is a subsequence of s[:i]. The empty target can be formed in exactly one way (take nothing), so ways[i][0] = 1, and a non-empty target cannot be formed from an empty source, so ways[0][j] = 0 for j > 0. For the general case, either the character s[i-1] is not used, contributing ways[i-1][j], or it is matched with t[j-1] (only possible when they are equal), contributing ways[i-1][j-1].

Each row depends only on the previous one, so a single array of length len(t)+1 suffices as long as the inner loop runs from high j to low j; this avoids using the character s[i-1] twice. Time is O(|s| · |t|), about a million updates for the largest input. Plain recursion without memoisation repeats the same sub-problems and is exponential.

title: Shortest Palindrome Length
desc:
You may add characters only at the front of the string s; nothing can be inserted in the middle or at the end. Find the shortest palindrome you can create this way and return its length.

For example, for s = "aacecaaa" you can prepend a single a to get "aaacecaaa", so the answer is 9. For s = "abcd" you must prepend "dcb" to get "dcbabcd", so the answer is 7. If s is already a palindrome the answer is len(s).
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters and digits
hints: Whatever you add is determined by how much of the start of s is already a palindrome.
If the longest palindromic prefix of s has length k, the remaining n - k characters must be mirrored in front, so the answer is 2n - k.

Find k in linear time with the KMP prefix function on s + '#' + reverse(s): the last value of the prefix function is the length of the longest prefix of s that equals a suffix of reverse(s), i.e. a palindromic prefix.
editorial: Let k be the length of the longest prefix of s that is a palindrome. The characters after that prefix cannot be part of the palindromic core, so their reverse must be placed in front, giving a result of length n + (n - k) = 2n - k. Any shorter result would need a longer palindromic prefix, contradicting maximality of k.

Checking every prefix for palindromicity costs O(n²), acceptable only for small inputs. To get O(n), build t = s + '#' + reverse(s) and compute the KMP failure (prefix) function. The final value pi[-1] is exactly k: a prefix of s that matches a suffix of reverse(s) is a prefix that equals its own reversal. The separator keeps the match from crossing the boundary (the alphabet never contains #).

title: Split Array Largest Sum
desc: Split the non-negative integer array nums into exactly k non-empty contiguous pieces. The cost of a split is the largest piece sum. Return the smallest cost that any split can achieve.
hints: A dynamic programming over (prefix, pieces) works but is cubic in the straightforward form. Think about whether the answer itself can be searched for.
Fix a limit L and ask: can the array be cut into at most k pieces, each with sum ≤ L? A greedy sweep that extends each piece as far as possible answers this.

The answer is the smallest feasible L. Feasibility is monotonic, so binary search L between max(nums) and sum(nums). Note that using fewer pieces can always be turned into exactly k by splitting pieces further, which never raises the maximum.
editorial: Let feasible(L) be true when the array can be divided into at most k contiguous pieces with every sum ≤ L. The greedy check scans left to right, closing a piece when adding the next element would exceed L; it uses the minimum possible number of pieces for that limit.

If a limit works, a bigger one works too, so binary search on the answer between max(nums) (every element must fit in some piece) and sum(nums) (one piece). Having fewer than k pieces is fine: because k ≤ n, any piece with more than one element can be cut further without increasing the maximum, until exactly k pieces exist. Complexity is O(n log(sum)) time and O(1) space; a DP would cost O(k n2). Total sums stay below 109, inside 32-bit range.

title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
desc: Given an integer array nums that may contain negative numbers, and a positive integer k, return the length of the shortest non-empty contiguous subarray whose sum is at least k. If no such subarray exists, return -1.
hints: The classic shrinking window fails here because negative values mean that adding an element can lower the sum. Use prefix sums instead: you want the closest pair i < j with pre[j] - pre[i] ≥ k.
For a fixed j, a larger and closer i is always better. If pre[i1] ≥ pre[i2] with i1 > i2, then index i2 is useless.
Maintain a deque of indices with increasing prefix sums. At each j, pop from the front while pre[j] - pre[front] ≥ k (recording lengths), then pop from the back while pre[back] ≥ pre[j], then push j.
editorial: Let pre[0] = 0 and pre[j] = nums[0] + ... + nums[j-1]. We want the minimum j - i with i < j and pre[j] - pre[i] ≥ k.

Keep a deque of candidate start indices whose prefix sums are strictly increasing. When we reach j: (1) while the front index satisfies the condition, record j - front and pop it, since any later j would only give a longer length for that start; (2) while the back index has a prefix sum that is not smaller than pre[j], pop it, since j is a later and lower start that dominates it; (3) push j. Each index is pushed and popped once, so the algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(n) space.

title: Candy
desc:
Children stand in a line, and child i has rating ratings[i]. You must give every child at least one candy, and any child with a strictly higher rating than an adjacent neighbour (left or right) must receive strictly more candies than that neighbour. Equal ratings impose no constraint.

Return the minimum total number of candies you need to hand out.
hints: Handle the two directions separately. First think only about the constraint with the left neighbour.
Sweep left to right: if a child's rating is higher than the left neighbour's, give one more candy than that neighbour, otherwise start at 1.
Do a second sweep from right to left for the right-neighbour constraint, and for each child take the larger of the two requirements. The sum is the minimum.
editorial: The two rules, one about each neighbour, are independent lower bounds. Make an array left where left[i] is the length of the strictly increasing run ending at i (counting i), and an array right with the length of the strictly decreasing run starting at i. Child i needs at least max(left[i], right[i]) candies.

That bound is also sufficient: giving each child exactly the maximum satisfies both neighbour constraints, so it is optimal. Two passes and one extra array give O(n) time. A single pass tracking the lengths of the current up-slope and down-slope reduces the extra space to O(1).

title: IPO
desc:
A company wants to raise its capital before an IPO by completing at most k distinct projects. You start with capital w. Project i yields a pure profit of profits[i] but you may only start it when your current capital is at least capital[i]. Starting a project does not consume capital: when you finish it, its profit is simply added to your capital, and the finished project cannot be repeated.

Projects are done one after another. Return the maximum capital you can have after completing at most k projects.
hints: At every step, which projects are even allowed? Among those, which one would you pick?
Since profit never decreases your capital and capital only unlocks more projects, always picking the most profitable affordable project is safe.
Sort projects by required capital. Sweep a pointer to move every newly affordable project into a max-heap keyed by profit, then pop the best one, add its profit and repeat up to k times.
editorial: Greedy works here because finishing any project only increases capital, and a higher capital can never make an option disappear. So among all currently affordable projects the one with the largest profit is never a worse choice: it gives at least as much capital as any alternative, which unlocks at least as many future projects.

Implementation: sort the projects by capital requirement. For up to k rounds, push every project whose requirement is at most the current capital into a max-heap of profits (advancing a pointer through the sorted list), then pop the top and add it to the capital. If the heap is empty, no project is affordable and you stop. The cost is O(n log n + k log n).
solution:
import heapq

def findMaximizedCapital(k, w, profits, capital):
    projects = sorted(zip(capital, profits))
    heap = []
    i = 0
    n = len(projects)
    for _ in range(k):
        while i < n and projects[i][0] <= w:
            heapq.heappush(heap, -projects[i][1])
            i += 1
        if not heap:
            break
        w -= heapq.heappop(heap)
    return w

title: Number of Islands II
desc:
An m x n map starts as all water. You are given a list positions; the k-th entry [r, c] turns the water cell in row r, column c into land (if that cell is already land, nothing changes).

An island is a maximal group of land cells that are connected through shared sides (up, down, left, right; diagonals do not count).

Return an array whose k-th element is the number of islands right after the k-th operation has been applied.
constraints: positions[k] = [r, c] with 0 ≤ r < m and 0 ≤ c < n
The same cell may appear more than once
hints: Re-running a full flood fill after every operation is far too slow for big inputs. How can you update the count incrementally?
When a cell becomes land it forms a new island (count + 1), but it may then join up to four neighbouring islands.

Use union-find over cell indices r * n + c. After marking the new cell, union it with each land neighbour; every union that merges two different sets lowers the count by one. Skip cells that are already land.
editorial: Keep a union-find over the m * n cells plus a boolean land array and a running island count. For each position: if the cell is already land, just record the current count. Otherwise mark it as land, add one to the count (it is a new island on its own), then look at the four neighbours. For each neighbour that is land, find the two roots; if they differ, union them and subtract one from the count.

Each operation does at most four unions, and with path compression and union by size every find is almost constant time, so the total cost is about O(k · α(m · n)) for k operations, plus O(m · n) to set up. Repeated positions must be ignored: counting them again as new islands would be wrong.

title: Palindrome Partitioning II
desc:
Cut the string s into consecutive pieces so that every piece reads the same forwards and backwards (a palindrome). Each place where you split the string counts as one cut.

Return the minimum number of cuts needed. A string that is already a palindrome needs 0 cuts.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only
hints: Every single character is a palindrome, so some answer always exists (at most n - 1 cuts).
Let cuts[i] be the minimum cuts for the first i characters. The last piece s[j..i-1] must be a palindrome, giving cuts[i] = min(cuts[j] + 1) over such j. How can you test palindromes fast?
Instead of testing every substring, expand around each of the 2n-1 centres. Whenever s[l..r] is a palindrome, update cuts[r + 1] = min(cuts[r + 1], cuts[l] + 1).
editorial: Define cuts[i] as the minimum cuts for the prefix of length i, with cuts[0] = -1 so that a prefix that is itself one palindrome costs -1 + 1 = 0. Initialise cuts[i] = i - 1, the cost of cutting between all characters.

Every palindrome has a centre, either a character or a gap between two. Process centres from left to right; for each, grow the window outwards while the two end characters match. For every palindrome s[l..r] found, relax cuts[r + 1] with cuts[l] + 1. Because every palindrome ending before position l has its centre to the left of the current one, cuts[l] is already final when it is used. Total work is O(n²) with only O(n) memory, versus O(n²) memory for a full palindrome table.

title: Critical Connections in a Network
desc:
A network has n servers numbered 0 to n - 1, joined by undirected cables. connections[i] = [a, b] is a cable between servers a and b. Every server can reach every other server, directly or through other servers.

A cable is critical if removing it (and only it) leaves at least one pair of servers unable to reach each other.

Return all critical cables. Write each one as [a, b] with a < b. The rows may be listed in any order. If none is critical, return an empty list.
constraints: connections[i] = [a, b] with 0 ≤ a, b < n and a ≠ b
No pair of servers is joined by more than one cable
hints: A critical cable is a bridge. Trying to delete every edge and re-check connectivity costs O(E · (V + E)), which is too slow for large inputs.
Run a DFS and record for each node the time at which it was first visited. Then ask: from the subtree below an edge, can any node reach back to an ancestor above that edge?
Keep low[v], the smallest discovery time reachable from v's subtree using at most one back edge. A tree edge (u, v) is a bridge exactly when low[v] > disc[u].
editorial: Run a depth-first search that assigns each node a discovery time disc and computes low[v] = the smallest discovery time reachable from v's DFS subtree through tree edges followed by at most one non-tree (back) edge. When processing the child v of u over tree edge (u, v), after finishing v set low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]). For any other already-visited neighbour w (not the parent edge), set low[u] = min(low[u], disc[w]).

The edge (u, v) is a bridge exactly when low[v] > disc[u]: nothing in v's subtree can climb back to u or above, so the cable is the only link. This is Tarjan's bridge-finding algorithm, linear in nodes plus edges. Since depth can reach 1,000, an explicit stack (iterative DFS) avoids recursion limits. Normalise each bridge to [min, max] before returning.
solution:
def criticalConnections(n, connections):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(connections):
        adj[a].append((b, i))
        adj[b].append((a, i))
    disc = [-1] * n
    low = [0] * n
    out = []
    timer = 0
    disc[0] = low[0] = 0
    timer = 1
    stack = [(0, -1, 0)]  # node, edge id used to arrive, next neighbour index
    while stack:
        u, pe, k = stack.pop()
        if k < len(adj[u]):
            stack.append((u, pe, k + 1))
            v, eid = adj[u][k]
            if eid == pe:
                continue
            if disc[v] == -1:
                disc[v] = low[v] = timer
                timer += 1
                stack.append((v, eid, 0))
            else:
                low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v])
        elif stack:
            p = stack[-1][0]
            low[p] = min(low[p], low[u])
            if low[u] > disc[p]:
                out.append([min(p, u), max(p, u)])
    return out

title: Subarrays with Exactly K Distinct Values
desc:
Given an integer array nums and an integer k, count the contiguous subarrays that contain exactly k different values.

Subarrays are counted by position, so equal-looking subarrays at different places count separately.

For example, nums = [1, 2, 1, 2, 3] and k = 2 give 7.
hints: Counting subarrays with at most k distinct values is much easier than counting exactly k, because a sliding window behaves monotonically.
For a fixed right end, if a window of distinct count at most k is valid, every shorter window ending there is valid too. Count all of them at once.
The answer is atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1). Implement atMost with two pointers and a frequency map.
editorial: Define atMost(m) as the number of subarrays with at most m distinct values. A subarray has exactly k distinct values iff it has at most k but not at most k - 1, so the answer is atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1).

Compute atMost(m) with a sliding window and a frequency map: for each right end, add the new element, and while the window has more than m distinct values advance the left end, decrementing counts and dropping values that reach zero. The window [left, right] then has at most m distinct values, and every start between left and right works, contributing right - left + 1 subarrays. Each pointer moves at most n times, giving O(n) overall.
The answer can reach about n<sup>2</sup>/2, which is 2 * 10<sup>8</sup> for n = 20,000 and fits in 32 bits.

title: Count Subarrays with Equal 0s, 1s and 2s
desc:
The array nums contains only the values 0, 1 and 2. Count the contiguous subarrays in which the number of 0s, the number of 1s and the number of 2s are all equal.

Such a subarray must have a length divisible by 3. The empty subarray is not counted.

For example, [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2] gives 4.
hints: For two symbols, a running difference of counts works. How can the same idea extend to three symbols?
Keep prefix counts c0, c1, c2. A subarray is balanced iff the three prefix counts grew by the same amount between its two ends.

Equal growth means the differences between counts stay unchanged, so use the pair (c1 - c0, c2 - c1) as a key. Two prefixes with the same pair delimit a balanced subarray; count equal keys in a hash map.
editorial: Let (c0, c1, c2) be the number of each symbol in the prefix. A subarray between prefix i and prefix j has all three counts equal exactly when c0[j] - c0[i] = c1[j] - c1[i] = c2[j] - c2[i]. Rearranging, this is the same as c1[j] - c0[j] = c1[i] - c0[i] and c2[j] - c1[j] = c2[i] - c1[i].

So each prefix is summarised by the key (c1 - c0, c2 - c1), and balanced subarrays correspond to pairs of prefixes with equal keys. Keep a hash map from key to the number of earlier prefixes with that key, seeded with the empty prefix key (0, 0). For each position add the current count of its key to the answer, then increment it. The empty subarray is never counted because we only pair a prefix with strictly earlier ones.
Time and space are O(n). The answer is at most about n<sup>2</sup>/6 and fits comfortably in 32 bits.

title: Max Overlap After Each Booking
desc:
A hall receives booking requests one at a time. Each request is a half-open time range [start, end): it occupies every moment t with start ≤ t < end, so two bookings that merely meet (one ends exactly when the other starts) do not overlap.

Process the requests in the given order. After each request has been added, report the largest number of bookings that cover one common moment (considering all requests accepted so far; every request is accepted). Return these maxima as an array with one entry per request.

bookings = [[10, 20], [50, 60], [10, 40], [5, 15], [5, 10], [25, 55]]
result = [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3]
hints: After each request the answer can only stay the same or grow, and it can grow by at most one. Only the moments inside the new range can have changed.
Coordinates go up to 10<sup>9</sup>, but only the 2n distinct endpoints matter. Compress them so that each gap between two consecutive endpoints is one cell holding a count.

Each booking is a range add of +1 on cells and you need the maximum cell after every insertion. A segment tree with lazy range add and a max query solves it in O(log n) per booking; the answer is the maximum stored in the root.
editorial: Between two consecutive distinct endpoints the number of active bookings is constant, so compress the up to 2n endpoints to ranks and work on the n' = (number of distinct endpoints - 1) elementary cells. A booking [s, e) covers the cells with ranks rank(s) .. rank(e) - 1.

The task is now: repeat a range add of +1 on cells, and after each add report the global maximum. A segment tree with range add and a stored maximum per node does exactly that. Use the non-propagating lazy form: each node keeps add (a pending increment applying to its whole range) and mx = add + max(mx of children). An update that fully covers a node just bumps both values; otherwise recurse and recompute. The answer after a booking is the root's mx.

That gives O(n log n) overall. A simpler approach keeps a sorted map of boundary changes and sweeps through all of it for every booking, which is O(n<sup>2</sup>) and is acceptable for n = 2,000 in compiled languages but slower in scripting languages; the tree is the version that scales.

title: Count Subarrays With Sum in Range
desc:
Given an integer array nums and two bounds lower and upper, count the contiguous non-empty subarrays whose sum S satisfies lower ≤ S ≤ upper. Subarrays at different positions are counted separately even if they have equal contents.

The array can contain negative numbers, so a sliding window does not work.

nums = [2, -3, 1, 4], lower = 0, upper = 3
result = 5   ([2], [1], [2,-3,1], [-3,1,4], [2,-3,1,4])
hints: Checking every pair (i, j) with a running sum is O(n2). With n = 10,000 that is 50 million sums, which is borderline; look for something better.
With prefix sums P (where P[0] = 0), the sum of nums[i..j-1] is P[j] - P[i]. For each j you need to count earlier i with P[j] - upper ≤ P[i] ≤ P[j] - lower.

Sweep j from left to right while keeping all earlier prefix sums in a structure that can count values in a range: a Fenwick tree over the compressed prefix values, or a merge sort that counts cross-half pairs.
editorial: Let P[0] = 0 and P[k] = nums[0] + ... + nums[k-1]. A subarray covering nums[i..j-1] has sum P[j] - P[i] with i < j. So the task is to count pairs of indices i < j with lower ≤ P[j] - P[i] ≤ upper, equivalently P[i] in the interval [P[j] - upper, P[j] - lower].

Process j in order, with all P[i] for i < j already inserted into a data structure that supports 'insert a value' and 'how many stored values lie in [x, y]'. Prefix sums can reach 1010 in absolute value, so compress them into ranks first (sort the distinct values) and use a Fenwick tree over the ranks; the interval bounds are mapped to ranks with binary search (bisect_left for the lower end, bisect_right for the upper end).

Total time is O(n log n). An equally good alternative is to run merge sort on the prefix array: while merging two sorted halves, two moving pointers count, for each element of the right half, how many left-half values fall inside the allowed interval. Brute force over all pairs is O(n<sup>2</sup>).
solution:
import bisect


def countRangeSum(nums, lower, upper):
    pre = [0]
    for x in nums:
        pre.append(pre[-1] + x)
    vals = sorted(set(pre))
    size = len(vals)
    tree = [0] * (size + 1)

    def add(pos):
        pos += 1
        while pos <= size:
            tree[pos] += 1
            pos += pos & -pos

    def query(cnt):  # number of inserted values among the first cnt ranks
        total = 0
        while cnt > 0:
            total += tree[cnt]
            cnt -= cnt & -cnt
        return total

    add(bisect.bisect_left(vals, 0))
    ans = 0
    for j in range(1, len(pre)):
        lo = bisect.bisect_left(vals, pre[j] - upper)
        hi = bisect.bisect_right(vals, pre[j] - lower)
        ans += query(hi) - query(lo)
        add(bisect.bisect_left(vals, pre[j]))
    return ans

title: Shortest Window Containing a Subsequence
desc:
You are given two integer arrays, nums and pattern. Find the shortest contiguous subarray of nums in which pattern appears as a subsequence, that is, you can pick the pattern's values in order from the subarray, skipping any elements in between.

Return the length of that shortest subarray, or -1 if no subarray works. Only the length is asked for, so ties between different windows do not matter.

nums = [1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 2, 5, 4], pattern = [3, 2, 4]
subarray [3, 2, 4] (positions 1 to 3) works
result = 3
hints: Checking every subarray against the pattern is far too slow. Start from a smarter question: for a fixed ending position, which start gives the shortest window?
Scan forward matching the pattern greedily until it is fully matched. That gives a valid end. Now walk backward from that end, matching the pattern in reverse, to find the latest possible start.

After recording the window, restart the forward scan from just after that start (not from the end). Repeat until the forward scan can no longer complete the pattern, and keep the smallest length seen.
editorial: Scan forward with a pointer into the pattern, advancing it whenever the current element matches. When the whole pattern is matched at index end, the window [?, end] is valid for some start, but the start found by the forward scan is not necessarily the tightest. Walk backward from end, matching the pattern from its last element to its first; the position where the backward walk finishes is the latest start for which a valid window ends at end. Record end - start + 1.

Next, continue the search from start + 1: any better window must start after the current start (a window starting at start or earlier cannot beat it for the same end region). Repeat until the forward scan runs out of array. This works in roughly O(n * m) time in the worst case (n = array length, m = pattern length) with O(1) extra space. A dynamic programming formulation that stores, for every pattern prefix, the latest start of a match is equivalent and gives the same O(n * m) bound.

title: Minimum K-Window Flips to All Ones
desc:
The array nums contains only 0 and 1. One operation picks any block of exactly k consecutive elements and flips every bit in it (0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0).

Return the minimum number of operations needed to make every element equal to 1, or -1 if it is impossible.

nums = [0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0], k = 3
flip [0..2] -> 1 1 1 1 0 1 1 0
flip [4..6] -> 1 1 1 1 1 0 0 0
flip [5..7] -> 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1
result = 3
hints: Flipping the same block twice cancels out, and the order of flips does not matter. So each starting position is either used once or not at all.
Look at the leftmost 0. Only a block starting exactly at that position can fix it without touching anything further left, so that flip is forced.

Sweep left to right with a greedy rule. To know the current state of a bit quickly, track how many active flips cover it (only the parity matters) and schedule the end of each flip with a difference array or a queue.
editorial: Because flips commute and cancel in pairs, the final state depends only on which start positions are used. Process positions from left to right. When you reach index i, its current value is its original value XOR the parity of the flips that cover it. If it is 0, the only block that can repair it without disturbing earlier, already fixed positions starts at i, so flipping there is forced. If i + k > n such a block does not fit, and the answer is -1.

Track the number of covering flips as a running parity: toggle it when you start a flip at i, and toggle it back at index i + k using a difference array of size n + 1. Every index is visited once, so the time is O(n) and the space is O(n). Because every flip is forced, the count is minimal.

title: Kth Smallest Pair Gap
desc:
For an integer array nums, the gap of a pair of positions i < j is |nums[i] - nums[j]|. There are n(n-1)/2 such pairs, and different pairs may have the same gap.

List the gaps of all pairs in non-decreasing order and return the k-th one (1-indexed). The array can be long, so enumerating all pairs is too slow.
hints: Generating all pairs and sorting needs O(n2) memory and time. Think about the answer's value instead of enumerating the pairs.
Sort the array first. For a candidate gap d, can you count the pairs with gap at most d in about O(n) time?

With the array sorted, the left end of the window [left, right] of elements within d of nums[right] only moves right as right grows, so a two-pointer sweep counts pairs. Binary search the smallest d in [0, max - min] whose count is at least k.
editorial: After sorting, the gap of a pair is just the difference of its values, and the gap between positions i < j is non-decreasing as the pair spreads apart. Let count(d) be the number of pairs with gap ≤ d. It is monotone in d, and the answer is the smallest d with count(d) ≥ k; at that point the answer is necessarily an actual gap, because the count only increases at gap values that occur.

To compute count(d), sweep right over the sorted array while keeping left as the first index with nums[right] - nums[left] ≤ d. Every index in [left, right - 1] forms a valid pair with right, adding right - left to the total. Since left never moves backwards, the sweep is O(n). The search over d takes about 31 iterations, for O(n log n + n log(max - min)) time and O(1) extra space after sorting. The largest possible gap is 2·109, which still fits in a signed 32-bit integer.
time: O(n log n + n log R)

title: Minimize the Largest Gap After Adding Stations
desc:
Fuel stations stand at the strictly increasing integer coordinates in stations along a straight road. You may build k additional stations, each at any integer coordinate (several may share a segment between two existing stations, but two stations cannot be at the same point).

After building, look at the distances between consecutive stations. Return the smallest possible value of the largest such distance. If there is only one station, there are no distances and the answer is 0.
hints: Only the gaps between neighbouring stations matter, and the new stations for one gap are independent of the others except for sharing the budget k.
Fix a target maximum gap D. A gap of length g needs the fewest extra stations when it is cut into parts of length at most D. How many stations is that?
A gap g needs ceil(g / D) - 1 new stations, i.e. (g - 1) // D. Binary search the smallest D from 1 to the largest gap such that the total needed over all gaps is at most k.
editorial: The largest gap is a lower-bounded-by-1 integer that never gets worse when more stations are allowed, so the question is: for a given D, what is the minimum number of new stations that makes every gap at most D? A gap of length g split into t equal-as-possible integer pieces has largest piece ceil(g / t), so it needs ceil(g / D) - 1 = (g - 1) // D new stations (zero when g ≤ D). Summing over all gaps gives need(D).

need(D) decreases as D grows, so binary search the smallest D in [1, maxGap] with need(D) ≤ k. Note that D = 1 is the floor because stations sit at distinct integer points. With a single station the answer is 0. Complexity: O(n log(maxGap)) time, O(1) extra space. The sum of needs can be as large as about 109, so use a type that holds it (in 32-bit languages it still fits, since the gaps sum to at most 109).

title: Maximal Rectangle of Ones
desc: A grid matrix contains only 0 and 1. Find the largest axis-aligned rectangle that is made up entirely of 1 cells and return its area (the number of cells it covers). If the grid has no 1, return 0.
constraints: All rows have the same length
hints: Try enumerating all rectangles first and see how expensive it is, then think about fixing the bottom edge row by row.
For a fixed bottom row, let h[c] be the number of consecutive 1s ending at that row in column c. The best rectangle with that bottom edge is the largest rectangle in the histogram h.

Update h row by row in O(columns), and solve each histogram with a monotonic stack of increasing heights: when a bar is lower than the top, pop and compute the area using the popped height and the width back to the new stack top.
editorial: Every all-ones rectangle has a bottom row. Process the grid row by row and maintain h[c], the height of the run of 1s that ends at the current row in column c (reset to 0 on a 0 cell). A rectangle whose bottom edge lies on the current row corresponds exactly to a contiguous range of columns and a height that is at most the minimum of h over that range, so we need the largest rectangle under the histogram h.

The largest-rectangle-in-histogram problem is solved with a stack of indices whose heights are increasing. When a bar of height h[c] is not taller than the bar on top, pop the top: its height can no longer extend to the right, its left boundary is the new top of the stack (or the start), so its area is height * (c - newTop - 1). A sentinel bar of height 0 after the last column flushes the stack. Each row costs O(columns), so the total is O(rows * columns), with O(columns) extra space.

title: Evaluate a Bracketed Arithmetic Expression
desc:
The string expr is a valid arithmetic expression with no spaces. It is built from non-negative integer literals, the binary operators +, - and *, and round brackets ( ) for grouping. Multiplication has higher priority than addition and subtraction, operators of the same priority are applied from left to right, and brackets override priority.

The minus sign may also appear as a unary operator, but only at the very start of the whole expression or immediately after an opening bracket, for example -(2+3)*4 or 5*(-3+1). It then negates the whole term that follows it (-2*3 is -6).

Evaluate the expression and return its value. You may not use any built-in function that evaluates a string as an expression.
constraints: expr contains only digits, '+', '-', '*', '(' and ')' and is a valid expression as described above
Every integer literal is between 0 and 1,000,000,000 and has no leading zeros (except the single digit "0")
Brackets are nested at most 300 levels deep
The value of every literal, product, partial sum and bracketed sub-expression met during evaluation has absolute value at most 2<sup>31</sup> - 1
hints: Plain left-to-right evaluation fails because of priority, and brackets make it recursive. Think about what you must remember when you enter a bracket.
Evaluate the current bracket level with a running total of finished terms, the value of the current product, and the sign of the current term. A closed bracket then behaves like a single number.

On '(' push the current state (total, current product, sign, whether a * is pending) on a stack and start fresh. On ')' finish the inner value, restore the saved state, and feed the value in as if it were a number. Remember the unary minus: a '-' when no term has started is just the sign of the first term.
editorial: Scan the string once. For each bracket level keep four things: total (the sum of completed terms), cur (the product of the factors of the current term seen so far, or none), sign (+1 or -1 for the current term) and mul (whether a * is waiting for its right operand). A number or a closed bracket is a value: if mul is set then cur *= value, otherwise cur = value.

On '+' or '-', first add the finished term sign * cur to total (if there is a term; at the start of an expression or just after '(' there is none, which is exactly the unary-minus case), then set the new sign. On '(' push (total, cur, sign, mul) and reset the four variables. On ')' compute total + sign * cur, restore the saved state from the stack and treat the result as a value. At the end the answer is total + sign * cur. Each character is handled once, so the time is O(n) and the stack holds at most one frame per open bracket.
solution:
def evaluateExpression(expr):
    stack = []
    total, cur, sign, mul = 0, None, 1, False
    n = len(expr)
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        c = expr[i]
        if c == "(":
            stack.append((total, cur, sign, mul))
            total, cur, sign, mul = 0, None, 1, False
            i += 1
            continue
        if c == "*":
            mul = True
            i += 1
            continue
        if c == "+" or c == "-":
            if cur is not None:
                total += sign * cur
                cur = None
            sign = 1 if c == "+" else -1
            i += 1
            continue
        if c == ")":
            value = total + sign * cur
            total, cur, sign, mul = stack.pop()
            i += 1
        else:
            j = i
            while j < n and expr[j].isdigit():
                j += 1
            value = int(expr[i:j])
            i = j
        if mul:
            cur *= value
            mul = False
        else:
            cur = value
    return total + sign * cur

title: Minimum Window Subsequence Length
desc:
Find the shortest contiguous substring (window) of s that contains t as a subsequence, that is, all characters of t appear inside the window in the same order, though not necessarily next to each other. Return the length of that window, or 0 if no window works.

For example, for s = "abcdebdde" and t = "bde" the answer is 4 (the window "bcde"). For s = "axbxc" and t = "abc" the answer is 5, and for s = "abc" and t = "ca" it is 0.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase letters and digits
hints: Checking every substring of s for the subsequence property is far too slow. First think about the cheaper question: for a fixed end position, where is the best place to start?
For each prefix of t of length j, track the largest start index such that t[0..j) is a subsequence of the window starting there and ending at the current position of s.

When you read s[i] and it equals t[j-1], the best start for prefix j becomes the best start for prefix j-1 (as it was before this character). Process j in decreasing order so a character is not used twice. Whenever the full t has a start, i - start + 1 is a candidate window.
editorial: Let start[j] be the maximum index p such that t[0..j) is a subsequence of s[p..i], or -1 if none exists. Reading the next character s[i], for every j with t[j-1] == s[i] we can finish prefix j here, using the best start of prefix j-1 from before: start[j] = start[j-1] (for j = 1 the start is simply i). Updating j from high to low prevents the same character of s from matching two positions of t.

Each time start[m] (m = len(t)) is set, the window [start[m], i] is a candidate and the shortest candidate is the answer. Keeping the latest start is right because a later start only shortens the window. The cost is O(|s| · |t|) in the worst case; indexing, for every character, the positions in t where it occurs lets the loop skip non-matching j. A naive search that tries all starts and greedily matches is O(|s|²) and too slow at 10,000.

title: Longest Duplicate Substring Length
desc:
Find the length of the longest substring of s that occurs at least twice in s. The two occurrences may overlap, but they must start at different positions. If no substring repeats, return 0.

For example, "banana" gives 3 ("ana" occurs at positions 1 and 3, overlapping), "abcd" gives 0, and "aaaa" gives 3.
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters and digits
hints: Comparing every pair of start positions character by character can take O(n³) in total. Suppose someone told you a length L: how would you test whether some substring of length L repeats?
If a substring of length L occurs twice, then so does every shorter prefix of it. So the property 'some duplicate of length L exists' is monotonic in L, and you can binary search on L.

To test a single L in linear time, slide a window of length L along the string and keep a rolling hash of the window in a map from hash to start positions. When a hash is seen again, compare the actual substrings to rule out collisions.
editorial: Binary search the answer. If a duplicate of length L exists, cutting one character off both copies gives a duplicate of length L-1, so feasibility is monotonic. The search range is 0 to n-1, taking about 15 steps for n = 20,000.

Each feasibility check slides a window across the string while maintaining a polynomial rolling hash modulo a large prime: when the window moves, remove the contribution of the outgoing character, multiply by the base and add the incoming character. Hash values are stored in a dictionary together with their start indices; on a hash hit, compare the two substrings directly so a collision can never produce a wrong answer. The expected cost of the whole algorithm is O(n log n).
Alternatives are a suffix array with an LCP array (the answer is the maximum LCP value) or a suffix automaton, both of which give deterministic bounds without hashing.

title: Count Distinct Substrings
desc:
Return the number of different non-empty substrings of s. Two substrings are the same if they consist of the same characters in the same order, no matter where in s they occur.

For example, "aaa" has the 3 distinct substrings "a", "aa", "aaa", and "abab" has 7: a, b, ab, ba, aba, bab, abab.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
The answer is at most n(n+1)/2, which is below 2<sup>31</sup>
hints: Putting every substring into a set needs O(n²) strings, each up to n long. That is far too much at n = 20,000.
Each substring is a prefix of some suffix. If you sort the suffixes, the number of new substrings a suffix contributes depends only on how much it shares with its neighbour in sorted order.

Either use a suffix array with the LCP array (answer = n(n+1)/2 minus the sum of LCPs), or build a suffix automaton: every state v represents len[v] - len[link[v]] distinct substrings, and the answer is the sum over states.
editorial: Counting by brute force with a set of all slices is O(n³) time-ish and O(n²) memory, only usable for very short strings. A trie of all suffixes reduces the time to O(n²) but still creates up to n²/2 nodes.

Suffix array approach: sort the suffixes, compute the LCP of each adjacent pair (for instance with Kasai's algorithm). Every suffix of length L introduces L prefixes, but the first lcp of them already appeared as prefixes of the previous suffix in sorted order. So the answer is n(n+1)/2 - sum(lcp).

Suffix automaton approach: the automaton is the smallest DFA that accepts all suffixes, and can be built online in O(n) amortised time. Its states partition all substrings into classes; state v contains the substrings with lengths in (len[link[v]], len[v]], so it contributes len[v] - len[link[v]] distinct substrings. Summing over all non-root states gives the answer. The automaton has at most 2n states, so memory is O(n) for a fixed alphabet.
solution:
def countDistinctSubstrings(s):
    nxt = [{}]
    link = [-1]
    length = [0]
    last = 0
    for c in s:
        cur = len(nxt)
        nxt.append({})
        length.append(length[last] + 1)
        link.append(0)
        p = last
        while p != -1 and c not in nxt[p]:
            nxt[p][c] = cur
            p = link[p]
        if p == -1:
            link[cur] = 0
        else:
            q = nxt[p][c]
            if length[p] + 1 == length[q]:
                link[cur] = q
            else:
                clone = len(nxt)
                nxt.append(dict(nxt[q]))
                length.append(length[p] + 1)
                link.append(link[q])
                while p != -1 and nxt[p].get(c) == q:
                    nxt[p][c] = clone
                    p = link[p]
                link[q] = clone
                link[cur] = clone
        last = cur
    return sum(length[v] - length[link[v]] for v in range(1, len(nxt)))

title: Longest Shared Substring of Two Strings
desc:
Return the length of the longest string that appears as a contiguous substring in both a and b. If the two strings share no character, return 0.

For example, a = "xabcdy" and b = "zzabcdq" share "abcd", so the answer is 4. For a = "abc" and b = "def" the answer is 0. Note that a substring is contiguous, unlike a subsequence.
constraints: Both strings consist of lowercase English letters
hints: The classic dynamic programme dp[i][j] (length of the common suffix of a[:i] and b[:j]) takes O(|a| · |b|) time, which is 108 steps at the limit. Look for something near-linear.
If a shared substring of length L exists, then shared substrings of every smaller length exist too. That allows a binary search on L if you can test one length quickly.

A suffix automaton of a recognises exactly the substrings of a. Feed b through it character by character, keeping the current state and the length of the match; when a transition is missing, follow suffix links until one exists. The maximum match length seen is the answer.
editorial: The table DP compares every pair of positions: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 if a[i-1] == b[j-1], else 0, and the answer is the maximum entry. It needs O(|a| · |b|) time, which is too slow for the largest inputs here, although it is a good way to check a faster method on small cases.

Binary search with hashing is one faster route: for a candidate length L, put the hashes of all length-L windows of a into a set and look for a window of b with a hash in it. The test is monotone in L, giving O((|a| + |b|) log n) expected time.

The deterministic linear method builds the suffix automaton of a (at most 2|a| states, built online). Then walk through b with a state v and a length len: for each character c, while v has no transition on c and is not the root, set v = link[v] and len = length[v]; if a transition exists, move along it and increase len. At every step len is the longest suffix of the processed part of b that is a substring of a, so the answer is the largest len reached. Time O(|a| + |b|), space O(|a|).
solution:
def longestSharedSubstring(a, b):
    nxt = [{}]
    link = [-1]
    length = [0]
    last = 0
    for c in a:
        cur = len(nxt)
        nxt.append({})
        length.append(length[last] + 1)
        link.append(0)
        p = last
        while p != -1 and c not in nxt[p]:
            nxt[p][c] = cur
            p = link[p]
        if p == -1:
            link[cur] = 0
        else:
            q = nxt[p][c]
            if length[p] + 1 == length[q]:
                link[cur] = q
            else:
                clone = len(nxt)
                nxt.append(dict(nxt[q]))
                length.append(length[p] + 1)
                link.append(link[q])
                while p != -1 and nxt[p].get(c) == q:
                    nxt[p][c] = clone
                    p = link[p]
                link[q] = clone
                link[cur] = clone
        last = cur
    v = 0
    cur_len = 0
    best = 0
    for c in b:
        while v != 0 and c not in nxt[v]:
            v = link[v]
            cur_len = length[v]
        if c in nxt[v]:
            v = nxt[v][c]
            cur_len += 1
        if cur_len > best:
            best = cur_len
    return best

title: Stock Profit with At Most K Transactions
desc:
prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You may complete at most k transactions, where one transaction is one purchase followed by one later sale of a single share. You can hold at most one share at a time, so you must sell before buying again (selling and buying again on the same day is allowed).

Return the maximum profit you can achieve; if no profitable transaction exists, the answer is 0.
hints: Decide per day among three actions: buy, sell, or do nothing. What do you need to remember to make that decision later?

Track two quantities per number of completed/started transactions j: buy[j], the best balance while holding a share bought in your j-th transaction, and sell[j], the best balance after completing j transactions.

Process prices left to right and update buy[j] = max(buy[j], sell[j-1] - p) and sell[j] = max(sell[j], buy[j] + p) for every j from 1 to k. If k ≥ n/2 the limit is irrelevant: just add up every positive day-to-day gain.
editorial: Think of each day as a state machine: either you hold no share or you hold one. Let sell[j] be the best cash balance after completing exactly j transactions (flat position) and buy[j] the best balance while holding a share from your j-th transaction. A new price p lets you buy (buy[j] = max(buy[j], sell[j-1] - p)) or sell (sell[j] = max(sell[j], buy[j] + p)). Initialise sell[0] = 0, every buy[j] to negative infinity and the rest of sell to 0 (fewer transactions than allowed is fine). After all days, sell[k] is the answer.

Each day costs O(k) updates, so the total is O(n × k) time with O(k) memory. One transaction needs at least two days, so with more than n/2 transactions the limit never binds; in that case the best profit is the sum of all positive differences between consecutive days, which keeps time and memory O(n) even for huge k.

title: Three Non-Overlapping Windows
desc:
A window is a block of exactly k consecutive elements of nums. Choose three windows that do not share any index (they may be adjacent) so that the total of all the elements inside them is as large as possible, and return that largest total.

It is guaranteed that nums.length ≥ 3 * k, so three windows always fit.
hints: Prefix sums let you get the sum of any window of length k in O(1). Let w[i] be the sum of the window starting at index i.
Three windows are ordered left to right: starts a, b, c with a + k ≤ b and b + k ≤ c. Fix the middle window b and think about the best choices to its left and right separately.
Precompute left[i] = the best w[a] with a ≤ i and right[i] = the best w[c] with c ≥ i. Then the answer is the maximum over b of left[b - k] + w[b] + right[b + k].
editorial: Let w[i] be the sum of nums[i..i+k-1], computed in O(n) with a running sum. Any valid selection has windows at starts a < b < c with b ≥ a + k and c ≥ b + k. Fix the middle start b: the best first window is the maximum of w[a] over a ≤ b - k, and the best third is the maximum of w[c] over c ≥ b + k.

Both of those are running maxima, so build left[i] = max(w[0..i]) and right[i] = max(w[i..end]) in one pass each. Then iterate b from k up to the last start that still leaves room for a third window, and take the maximum of left[b - k] + w[b] + right[b + k]. Everything is O(n) time and O(n) space. The answer is a sum, so there is no ambiguity even when several choices tie.

title: Dungeon Minimum Starting Health
desc:
A knight must cross a rectangular dungeon from the top-left room to the bottom-right room, moving only right or down. Entering a room changes his health by that room's value: a negative number is damage, a positive number is a healing potion, and 0 changes nothing. The first and the last room also apply their value.

The knight dies the moment his health becomes 0 or less, even in the final room. Return the smallest positive starting health that lets him complete the crossing along some route.
constraints: The knight's health must stay at least 1 after entering every room
hints: Running a forward DP over 'minimum health needed so far' is tricky because two quantities matter: the current health and the lowest point reached. Try going backwards.
Let need[r][c] be the minimum health required on entering room (r, c) to survive the rest of the trip to the end.
At the end room need = max(1, 1 - value). Elsewhere, need[r][c] = max(1, min(need[r+1][c], need[r][c+1]) - value[r][c]). The answer is need[0][0].
editorial: A forward DP does not work, because a route with a large sum so far but a deep dip earlier is not comparable to one with a smaller sum and no dip. Reversing the direction fixes this: define need[r][c] as the least health with which the knight can enter room (r, c) and still finish alive. It depends only on the future, which is exactly what the knight must survive.

In the last room the health after entering must be at least 1, so need = max(1, 1 - value). In another room the health after entering is h + value, and it must be at least the smaller requirement of the two next rooms, so h ≥ min(need[r+1][c], need[r][c+1]) - value; clamp this to at least 1 because health must always be positive. Fill the table from the bottom-right corner back to the top-left in O(m · n) time and O(n) space.

title: Two Robots Cherry Collection
desc:
An orchard is a grid with rows rows and cols columns; grid[r][c] is the number of cherries lying in that cell. Two robots work together. Robot 1 starts in the top-left cell (0, 0) and robot 2 starts in the top-right cell (0, cols - 1).

The robots move in lockstep, one row down per step. From column c, each robot independently moves to column c - 1, c or c + 1 in the next row, never leaving the grid. Each robot picks up all the cherries in every cell it stands on, including its starting cell. If both robots are in the same cell, the cherries there are only collected once. Both robots stop in the last row.

Return the maximum total number of cherries the robots can collect.
constraints: When cols == 1 both robots start in the same cell
hints: Two robots in the same row means the situation at any moment is described by the row and the two columns. Moving them one after another instead of together would need far more state.
Define f[r][a][b] as the most cherries both robots can still collect from row r down, when robot 1 is in column a and robot 2 in column b.
f[r][a][b] = cells(r, a, b) + max f[r+1][a'][b'] over the 9 combinations a' in {a-1,a,a+1}, b' in {b-1,b,b+1}, where cells adds the cherries of both columns but counts a shared cell once.
editorial: Because both robots descend exactly one row per step, the pair (column of robot 1, column of robot 2) fully describes the future once the row is known. There are at most cols<sup>2</sup> such pairs per row, and each has 9 successors, so a DP over rows is cheap even though the number of joint routes is astronomical.

Work from the last row upwards: f[last][a][b] = cells(last, a, b), and for earlier rows add the best successor value. The value of a cell pair is grid[r][a] + grid[r][b] if a != b, else just grid[r][a]; this is what handles the 'collected only once' rule. The answer is f[0][0][cols-1]. Only two layers of the table are needed at any time, so memory is O(cols2) and time O(rows · cols2 · 9).

title: Merge Stones into One Pile
desc:
There are n piles of stones in a row, and stones[i] is the number of stones in pile i. In one move you pick exactly k consecutive piles and merge them into a single pile. The cost of the move is the total number of stones in those k piles, and the new pile holds that many stones.

Return the minimum total cost of merging all the piles into one single pile, or -1 if it is impossible.
hints: Each merge reduces the pile count by k - 1. When can n piles ever become exactly 1 pile?
Use interval DP. Let dp[i][j] be the minimum cost to merge piles i..j into as few piles as possible. Think about where the first merged group ends.

Split [i, j] as [i, m] merged into one pile plus [m+1, j] reduced to (len - 1) mod (k - 1) piles; m advances in steps of k - 1. If the length of [i, j] minus 1 is divisible by k - 1, add the sum of the interval for the final merge.
editorial: Each move removes k - 1 piles, so one pile can be reached only if (n - 1) % (k - 1) == 0; otherwise the answer is -1.

Let dp[i][j] be the minimum cost to merge the piles i..j until no more merges are possible, which leaves (len - 1) % (k - 1) + 1 piles. Intervals shorter than k cost 0. For longer intervals, the leftmost remaining pile covers some prefix [i, m] that was merged into a single pile, so m - i is a multiple of k - 1, and the rest [m+1, j] is reduced independently: dp[i][j] = min over m of dp[i][m] + dp[m+1][j]. If the interval can collapse completely, i.e. (len - 1) % (k - 1) == 0, the last merge combines k piles holding the whole interval's stones, adding prefix[j+1] - prefix[i].
There are O(n<sup>2</sup>) intervals and about n / (k - 1) split points each, so the total time is O(n<sup>3</sup> / k) and space is O(n<sup>2</sup>).

title: Shortest Walk Visiting Every Node
desc:
An undirected, connected graph has n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1. It is given as an adjacency list: graph[i] lists every node that shares an edge with node i.

A walk may start at any node, may finish anywhere, and may revisit nodes and reuse edges as often as needed. Return the minimum number of edges in a walk that visits every node at least once.
constraints: graph[i] has no repeated values and never contains i
j is in graph[i] if and only if i is in graph[j]
hints: Because nodes may be revisited, a plain search over simple paths is not enough. Which pieces of information must a search state remember?
A state is (set of visited nodes, current node). With n ≤ 12 there are at most 2<sup>12</sup> · 12 states, which is small.

All edges cost 1, so run a breadth-first search on these states, starting from every node at once with only that node marked visited. The first time a state's mask is full, its distance is the answer.
editorial: Model the walk as a path in a state graph. A state is a pair (mask, u): mask is the set of nodes visited so far and u the current node. Moving along an edge u - v goes to (mask | (1 << v), v) and costs one edge. A state can be revisited with the same mask, which is why we keep a visited table over states rather than over nodes.

Since every transition costs 1, breadth-first search finds shortest distances. Start with all (1 << i, i) at distance 0 (the walk may begin anywhere) and stop at the first state whose mask has all n bits set. For a single node the answer is 0. There are n · 2n states and each expands over at most n neighbours, so the time is O(n2 · 2n).

title: Count Distinct Palindromic Subsequences
desc:
Given a string s made only of the letters a, b, c and d, count the distinct non-empty palindromic strings that can be obtained as a subsequence of s. Two subsequences that spell the same string count once, even if they use different indices.

The count can be huge, so return it modulo 1,000,000,007.

s = "bccb"  ->  6    (b, c, bb, cc, bcb, bccb)
s = "aaa"   ->  3    (a, aa, aaa)
s = "abcd"  ->  4
constraints: s contains only the characters 'a', 'b', 'c' and 'd'
hints: Count palindromes inside intervals: D(i, j) is the number of distinct non-empty palindromic subsequences of s[i..j]. If the end characters differ, use inclusion-exclusion over the two shorter intervals.

If the end characters are equal to c, every palindrome that starts and ends with c has the form c + X + c where X is empty or a palindrome from the inside, plus the single 'c'. Duplicates arise when c also occurs inside, so look at the first and last occurrence of c strictly inside the interval.

Let l and r be the first and last c strictly inside (i, j). None inside: 2 * D(i+1, j-1) + 2. Exactly one (l == r): 2 * D(i+1, j-1) + 1. Two or more: 2 * D(i+1, j-1) - D(l+1, r-1). Precompute previous/next occurrence arrays for O(1) lookup.
editorial: If s[i] != s[j], a palindrome in s[i..j] either avoids the left end or avoids the right end, so by inclusion-exclusion D[i][j] = D[i+1][j] + D[i][j-1] - D[i+1][j-1].

If s[i] == s[j] == c, the distinct palindromes of s[i..j] are the ones that already exist strictly inside, counted by D[i+1][j-1], plus new ones that wrap an inside palindrome in c: one string c X c for every inside palindrome X, and also c and cc (the empty X). That gives 2 * D[i+1][j-1] + 2 candidates, but some of them may already be present inside. Let l and r be the first and last occurrences of c strictly between i and j. If there is none, nothing is double counted: 2 * D[i+1][j-1] + 2. If there is exactly one, the string c is already inside: 2 * D[i+1][j-1] + 1. If there are two or more, both c and cc are already inside, and a string c X c is already inside exactly when X can be found between l and r, so subtract D[l+1][r-1] and drop the +2: 2 * D[i+1][j-1] - D[l+1][r-1].

Precompute for every index the next and previous index holding the same letter so each cell costs O(1). Total time is O(n²) with an n × n table (about a million cells), taking all values modulo 10<sup>9</sup>+7. Enumerating subsequences and inserting them into a set is exponential.

title: Scramble String
desc:
A string can be scrambled with this recursive procedure. If the string has length 1, stop. Otherwise cut it at some position into two non-empty parts x and y, optionally swap them so the string becomes y + x instead of x + y, and then apply the same procedure independently to each of the two parts (each part may use a different cut and a different swap decision).

Given two strings s1 and s2 of the same length, return true if s2 can be produced from s1 by some sequence of such choices.

s1 = "great", s2 = "rgeat"  ->  true
s1 = "abcde", s2 = "caebd"  ->  false
s1 = "a",     s2 = "a"      ->  true
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: If s2 is a scramble of s1, then at the top-level cut each half of s1 matches some block of s2 as a scramble. Which blocks of s2 can that be?

For a cut of length k there are two possibilities: no swap (the first k characters of s1 against the first k of s2, the rest against the rest) or swap (the first k of s1 against the last k of s2, the rest against the first part).
Memoise on (start in s1, start in s2, length). Prune quickly: two blocks can only be scrambles if they contain exactly the same multiset of letters, and equal blocks are trivially scrambles.
editorial: Let S(i, j, L) be true when s1[i:i+L] can be scrambled into s2[j:j+L]. A block of length 1 matches if the characters are equal. For longer blocks, try every cut k from 1 to L-1. Without a swap we need S(i, j, k) and S(i+k, j+k, L-k). With a swap the first part of s1 lands at the end of s2, so we need S(i, j+L-k, k) and S(i+k, j, L-k).

There are about n<sup>3</sup>/3 states and each tries up to n cuts, so the time is O(n<sup>4</sup>), which is tiny for n ≤ 40. Without memoisation the same sub-blocks are re-solved over and over and the search is exponential. Cheap pruning makes it much faster in practice: if the two blocks are identical return true immediately, and if their sorted letters differ return false, since scrambling only rearranges characters.

title: Minimum Obstacle Removal in a Grid
desc:
In a grid, a 0 is an empty cell and a 1 is an obstacle. You stand at the top-left cell and want to reach the bottom-right cell by moving up, down, left or right. You may walk through empty cells freely, and you may also break through an obstacle, which removes it and costs 1.

Return the minimum number of obstacles you have to remove to reach the bottom-right cell. Both the start and the target cell are empty.

grid = [[0,1,1],
        [1,1,0],
        [1,1,0]]   -> 2
hints: The shortest route in steps is not what matters: stepping on an empty cell is free and breaking an obstacle costs 1.
This is a shortest-path problem where entering a cell costs either 0 or 1. Dijkstra works. Can you do better using the fact that costs are only 0 and 1?
Use a deque: when moving to a cell of cost 0 push the cell at the front of the deque, for cost 1 push it at the back (0-1 BFS). Update a distance array only when you find a strictly smaller value.
editorial: Model each cell as a node and the cost of entering it as its value (0 or 1). The task is the cheapest path from the top-left to the bottom-right node. Plain BFS fails because edges have different weights, and Dijkstra is correct but pays a logarithmic factor for the heap.

With weights restricted to 0 and 1, a deque replaces the heap: pop a cell from the front, and for each neighbour try dist[cur] + grid[nb]; if that improves the stored distance, store it and push the neighbour on the front when the cost is 0, otherwise on the back. The deque always stays ordered by distance, so each cell settles after a constant number of improvements. Total time is O(rows × cols).

title: Swim in Rising Water
desc:
An n x n grid elevation holds the height of the ground at every cell; the heights are the distinct integers 0, 1, ..., n*n - 1, each used once. At time t the water level everywhere is exactly t.

You start at the top-left cell and want to reach the bottom-right cell. In zero time you can move to an adjacent cell (up, down, left or right) when both the cell you stand on and the cell you move to have height at most t. You may wait for the water to rise as long as you like. Return the smallest t at which the bottom-right cell can be reached.

elevation = [[0, 2],
             [1, 3]]   -> 3

At t = 3 every cell is flooded enough to walk along the top row and down; before that the target (height 3) is still above the water.
constraints: elevation is n x n and contains each of 0 .. n*n - 1 exactly once
hints: Walking a path is possible at time t iff the highest cell on the path is at most t. So you want a path whose highest cell is as low as possible.
One approach: guess a time t and test with BFS whether the target is reachable using only cells of height at most t. Reachability only gets easier as t grows.
Another: run a Dijkstra-like search with a min-heap keyed by the largest height seen on the way so far. The key of the target when it is first popped is the answer.
editorial: The time to complete a path equals the maximum height of any cell on it, including start and end. The answer is the minimum, over all paths, of that maximum (a minimax path).

A min-heap search handles it directly: start with (elevation[0][0], 0, 0), pop the smallest key, and push each unvisited neighbour with key max(key, height). Because keys come out of the heap in non-decreasing order, the first time the bottom-right cell is popped its key is the optimum. This costs O(n2 log n).
Alternatives: binary search on t with a BFS feasibility check (O(n2 log n)), or add cells in increasing height order into a disjoint-set union and stop when the start and end become connected.

title: Alien Dictionary Order
desc:
An alien language uses an alphabet of m letters, written here as the integers 0 to m - 1. The alien order of the letters is unknown. A dictionary of words (each word is an array of letters) is known to be listed in lexicographic order under that unknown alphabet order: comparing two words, look at the first position where they differ, and the word with the letter that comes earlier in the alien alphabet is the smaller one. If one word is a prefix of the other, the shorter word is smaller. Equal words may appear next to each other.

Return an ordering of all m letters (every letter from 0 to m - 1 exactly once) that is consistent with the dictionary. Letters the dictionary says nothing about must still appear. Because many orderings may be consistent, return the lexicographically smallest one when the orderings are compared as integer arrays. If the dictionary is contradictory, return an empty array.
hints: Only neighbouring words need comparing, and each such pair tells you at most one fact: the first differing letters give 'a comes before b'.

Those facts are edges of a directed graph on the letters, and an ordering that respects all of them is a topological order. Watch for the prefix trap: a longer word directly before its own prefix is impossible no matter what the alphabet is.

To get the smallest valid order, run Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap of the letters whose in-degree is zero instead of a plain queue. If fewer than m letters come out, there is a cycle: return an empty array.
editorial: Compare each adjacent pair of words. Scan to the first differing position; if there is one, add an edge a → b from the letter in the earlier word to the letter in the later one (once per distinct pair; duplicates would double-count the in-degree). If there is none, the words are equal up to the shorter length: that is fine when the first is the shorter or the same length, but when the first word is longer, it would have to sort after its own prefix, so the dictionary is invalid and the answer is empty.

Now any valid alphabet is a topological order of the graph over all m letters, including those with no edges at all. A plain topological sort could return any of them; the lexicographically smallest is produced by always taking the smallest available letter. Use a min-heap holding every letter whose in-degree has dropped to 0: pop the smallest, append it, and release its out-edges. Picking the smallest ready letter at each step is optimal because each choice only delays larger letters, never blocks smaller ones. If the output has fewer than m letters a cycle exists (for example 0, 1, 0 as three words) and the answer is []. Cost: O(L + m log m + E) where L is the total number of letters in the comparisons.

title: Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges of an MST
desc:
A connected, weighted, undirected graph has n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1. Each entry edges[i] = [a, b, w] joins nodes a and b with weight w. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is a set of n - 1 edges that connects all nodes and has the smallest possible total weight. Several different MSTs may exist when weights tie.

Classify every edge by its role across all minimum spanning trees:

  • 2 — critical: it belongs to every MST (removing it makes the cheapest spanning tree heavier, or impossible).
  • 1 — pseudo-critical: it belongs to at least one MST but not to all of them.
  • 0 — it belongs to no MST at all.

Return an array res of length edges.length where res[i] is the class of edges[i].
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b < n, a ≠ b, and each pair of nodes is joined by at most one edge
hints: Start by finding the weight W of an MST (Kruskal's algorithm). All MSTs share that weight, so you can test each edge by comparing against W.
An edge is critical if the best spanning tree that is forbidden from using it is heavier than W (or cannot exist at all).

If an edge is not critical, force it in: start the union-find with that edge already joined, run Kruskal on the rest, and compare. If the total is still W, some MST contains it (pseudo-critical); otherwise it is in none.
editorial: Compute W, the weight of an MST, with Kruskal's algorithm: sort the edges by weight and join components with union-find. Then examine each edge i separately, using the same routine with two options. Excluding edge i: skip it during Kruskal. If the tree is heavier than W or fails to connect all nodes, every MST must use edge i, so it is critical (2).

Otherwise some MST avoids edge i. Forcing edge i: union its endpoints first, add its weight, then run Kruskal over the other edges. If the total equals W, then there is an MST that contains edge i and one that does not, so it is pseudo-critical (1). If the forced tree is heavier than W, edge i is in no MST (0). Each test is one Kruskal pass over the sorted edges, so the whole algorithm is O(E · E · α(n)), about 80,000 steps for 200 edges.

It is worth seeing why forcing is sound: Kruskal on the remaining edges, after the forced edge is merged, returns the cheapest spanning tree that contains that edge, by the same exchange argument that proves ordinary Kruskal optimal. And a graph where all weights tie shows the three classes clearly: every non-bridge edge is pseudo-critical, every bridge is critical.

title: Binary Tree Cameras
desc:
You may place surveillance cameras on the nodes of a binary tree. A camera on a node watches that node itself, its parent and its children (but nothing further away). Return the minimum number of cameras needed so that every node of the tree is watched. The empty tree needs 0 cameras.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

Node values are irrelevant to the answer; only the shape matters. For tree = [0, 0, -1, 0, 0] the answer is 1 (a camera on the middle node covers all four nodes). For the chain [0, 0, -1, 0, -1, 0] of four nodes the answer is 2.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
Node values do not matter; only the shape of the tree does
hints: Think about the leaves. Is it ever better to put a camera on a leaf than on its parent?
